Paper Name: 3D Bioprinter Firmware Attacks: Categorization, Implementation, and Impacts
Attacks Mentioned: Firmware-based IP/data theft, persistent bootloader compromise (MalBoot), printer hardware sabotage, temperature manipulation, print-speed alteration, nozzle switching, contamination risks, and standoff-distance manipulation
Defence Mentioned: Recommended: Secure boot, cryptographic firmware signing, TPM/HSM-based authentication, secure supply chains, runtime monitoring, and access controls.
Contribution: Categorizes 26 potential firmware attacks and implements 10 on a real bioprinter, evaluating effects on printer hardware, printability, and cell viability.
Lifecycle stage: Firmware compromise during build execution; post-print quality and cell-viability assessment.
Threat Model: Supply-chain adversary has physical device access and access to firmware/bootloader source, enabling malicious firmware installation and persistence, with data theft and device/construct sabotage objectives.
Purdue Stage: L1 firmware and bootloader; L0 printer hardware
Paper Limitations: Physical supply-chain access and firmware-source access are assumptions; demonstrations use one extrusion-based bioprinter and A549 cells.

Paper Name: 3D Printer Audio and Vibration Side Channel Dataset for Vulnerability Research in Additive Manufacturing Security
University: University of Delaware, National Technical University of Athens
Attacks Mentioned: Acoustic and vibration side-channel attacks potentially enabling reconstruction of printing movements, design information theft, and counterfeiting.
Defence Mentioned: No new defense proposed or evaluated. Existing motor noise-cancellation and vibration-suppression features of the studied printers are discussed.
Contribution: Releases 288 audio/vibration data files collected from two Bambu Lab printers using an iPhone and Teensy 4.0, covering 12 printed objects, with corresponding design and toolpath files to support future vulnerability research.
Lifecycle stage: Side-channel information leakage during printing.
Threat Model: Dataset supports study of IP leakage from acoustic/vibration measurements using nearby iPhone or Teensy sensors; no particular adversary, access policy or successful reconstruction is established.
Purdue Stage: L0 printer motion, audio/vibration emissions and sensors; process signals may disclose L1 motion behavior.
Paper Limitations: Authors use two FDM printers and 12 objects; not a demonstrated reconstruction attack or validated defence.

Paper Name: A Blockchain-Based G-Code Protection Approach for Cyber-Physical Security in Additive Manufacturing
University: Oklahoma State University, The University of Texas at Arlington, Mississippi State University
Attacks Mentioned: Malicious G-code/design modifications, unauthorized toolpath manipulation, and intellectual property theft through G-code access.
Defence Mentioned: Blockchain-based G-code storage and asymmetric encryption to detect tampering and restrict unauthorized access.
Contribution: Proposes and evaluates a blockchain-encryption framework for G-code protection, demonstrating its application through an AM face-shield fabrication case study.
Lifecycle stage: G-code generation, storage, secure transfer, and protection before build execution.
Purdue Stage: L3 preparation/storage of G-code; blockchain data storage may be L5–L4
Paper Limitations: Need to read full paper

Paper Name: A correlation among industry 4.0, additive manufacturing, and topology optimization: a state-of-the-art review
Where When Published: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology; 2023
University: University of Engineering and Technology, Lahore, Missouri University of Science and Technology
Attacks Mentioned: General AM cybersecurity threats, data-privacy risks, IP protection concerns, and supply-chain cyberattack risks. No specific attack is experimentally demonstrated.
Defence Mentioned: Reviews ML-based attack detection, blockchain-based IP protection, intrusion detection, secure communication protocols, and access controls.
Contribution: Reviews the integration of Industry 4.0, topology optimization, and additive manufacturing, including design optimization, digital twins, manufacturing technologies, challenges, and a brief discussion of AM cybersecurity.
Lifecycle stage: Primarily digital design/optimization and connected manufacturing processes.
Threat Model: Surveys Industry 4.0, topology optimization and AM
Purdue Stage: L3 design/topology optimization and build preparation; L2–L0 connected equipment and physical manufacturing
Paper Limitations: Unresolved cybersecurity/privacy challenges and call for standards and research.

Paper Name: Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks on Additive Manufacturing Systems
Attacks Mentioned: Side-channel -> Acoustic attack
Contribution: Proposing a new attack methodology.
Lifecycle stage: Side-channel information leakage during printing.
Threat Model: Acoustic eavesdropper uses a nearby microphone and trained signal-learning models to infer movement axes, distance and G-code for IP reconstruction; no control of printer is required.
Purdue Stage: L0 stepper motors, motion and acoustic emissions, disclosing information about L1 printer control.
Paper Limitations: microphone distance, orientation and surrounding noise affect attack quality.

Paper Name: A cyber-physical attack taxonomy for production systems: a quality control perspective
Attacks Mentioned: IP theft, equipment sabotage, product dimensional manipulation, mechanical-property alteration, and attacks designed to evade quality-control (QC) systems.
Defence Mentioned: Traditional QC and inspection systems; emphasizes the need for more robust, attack-aware QC methods. Does not introduce a validated detection system
Contribution: Proposes a manufacturing cyber-physical attack taxonomy with four considerations: attack objective, affected components, attack method, and attack location.
Lifecycle stage: Production execution and quality inspection. Applicable to manufacturing broadly, not exclusively AM.
Threat Model: Taxonomy analyzes attacker objective, access, location and effect in production/QC systems
Purdue Stage: L2 quality-control monitoring and L1–L0 production equipment.

Paper Name: A Data Exfiltration and Remote Exploitation Attack on Consumer 3D Printers
Where When Published: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security; 2016
University: University of South Australia, University of Texas at San Antonio
Attacks Mentioned: Unauthorized extraction of stored print files, remote printer manipulation, exploitation of unauthenticated web services and flawed TLS implementations.
Defence Mentioned: Manufacturer-level and user-level security
Contribution: Investigates two MakerBot printer models, identifies security vulnerabilities, demonstrates an attack approach for data exfiltration and remote exploitation, and models the attack steps.
Lifecycle stage: Printer communication, stored print jobs, and remote machine control.
Threat Model: Attacker has ordinary client-level access to the same network but no elevated network privileges or physical access. They seek authentication codes and tokens to exfiltrate stored object data or remotely manipulate MakerBot printers.
Purdue Stage: L2 network-facing printer services, authentication and stored jobs; physical printer at L0 is downstream of remote control.

Paper Name: Additive Manufacturing Cyber-Physical System: Supply Chain Cybersecurity and Risks
University: New York University Tandon School of Engineering, Brooklyn, NY, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX
Attacks Mentioned: Design theft and modification, malware, ransomware, side-channel attacks, printer-parameter sabotage, raw-material tampering, reverse engineering, and counterfeit production.
Defence Mentioned: Encryption, watermarking, digital rights management (DRM), access controls, secure infrastructure, material provenance, and embedded product-authentication features.
Contribution: Proposes three AM supply-chain models, an expanded attack/risk classification, and a holistic analysis connecting digital-design, printer-hardware, and raw-material supply chains.
Lifecycle stage: Digital preparation, material supply, build execution, and product authentication.
Threat Model: Supply-chain analysis surveys attacks on design information, raw materials and printer hardware. Threat actors and access vary by the digital, material and hardware chain; no single attacker model.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 enterprise/supply-chain data, L3 digital preparation and L1–L0 machine/material handling
Paper Limitations: Supply-chain framework and prior-study synthesis

Paper Name: An LSTM-Autoencoder Based Online Side Channel Monitoring Approach for Cyber-Physical Attack Detection in Additive Manufacturing
University: Oklahoma State University, The University of Texas at Arlington, Mississippi State University
Attacks Mentioned: Malicious alterations to printed-part geometry and layer thickness.
Defence Mentioned: Online vibration-based side-channel monitoring using an LSTM-autoencoder, with supervised and unsupervised attack-detection schemes.
Contribution: Develops and experimentally evaluates an ML-based process-authentication method using two accelerometers on an FFF printer to detect geometry and layer-thickness alterations in real time.
Lifecycle stage: In-situ monitoring during build execution.
Threat Model: Two experimental process alterations mimic compromised part geometry and layer thickness on an FFF machine
Purdue Stage: L0 FFF machine vibrations and accelerometers; L2 supervisory online monitoring and anomaly analysis.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify the use of vibration only and simple part designs as limitations, requiring study of more complex toolpaths and other sensors.

Paper Name: A Non-Line-of-Sight, Multi-Modality-based Side-Channel IP Theft Attack on Additive Manufacturing Using Dual Smartphones
University: University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Lafayette, LA, Auburn University, Auburn, AL
Attacks Mentioned: Side-channel IP theft through acoustic and magnetic emissions, enabling unauthorized G-code reconstruction without direct printer access.
Defence Mentioned: Acoustic and electromagnetic shielding, printing-path randomization, active noise/jamming, and anomaly detection. These are discussed as countermeasures, not experimentally validated.
Contribution: Demonstrates a non-line-of-sight attack using two smartphones positioned 60 cm from a printer, achieving 98.89% G-code command reconstruction accuracy in a reported experiment.
Lifecycle stage: Information leakage during active printing
Threat Model: An eavesdropper positions two smartphones 60 cm away without line of sight, recording acoustic and magnetic emissions to reconstruct G-code and steal design IP.
Purdue Stage: L0 printer physical emissions observed externally, disclosing aspects of L1 motion commands.

Paper Name: An Online Side Channel Monitoring Approach for Cyber-Physical Attack Detection of Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Malicious part-geometry modifications and layer-thickness alterations.
Defence Mentioned: Online side-channel process authentication using accelerometer measurements, autoencoder-based feature extraction, and supervised/unsupervised monitoring.
Contribution: Proposes and evaluates an online attack-detection approach on an FFF printer equipped with two accelerometers, demonstrating real-time detection of two types of print alterations.
Lifecycle stage: In-situ attack monitoring during build execution.
Paper Limitations: Need to read full paper

Paper Name: A Novel Hierarchical Security Solution for Controller-Area-Network-Based 3D Printing in a Post-Quantum World
Attacks Mentioned: CAN message manipulation, eavesdropping, replay attacks, device impersonation, hardware Trojans, fuzzing, and denial-of-service attacks.
Defence Mentioned: Hierarchical CAN subnet isolation, root-of-trust authentication, authenticated encryption, and lightweight/post-quantum cryptographic schemes.
Contribution: Develops a secure hierarchical CAN architecture supporting legacy devices. Its implementation reports approximately 25% and 90% fewer authentication messages than compared lightweight and post-quantum CAN security solutions, respectively.
Lifecycle stage: Printer-controller communications and execution-time network security.
Threat Model: Addresses malicious CAN-node traffic and hardware Trojans that may eavesdrop, spoof, replay, fuzz, impersonate or disrupt printer communications; architecture isolates affected subnets and assumes authentication/key mechanisms.
Purdue Stage: L1 CAN devices, routing and controller communication; L0 connected printer sensors and actuators; L2 supervisory root when deployed.
Paper Limitations: DoS containment is partial to affected subnets and suggest future software/hardware acceleration and comparative cryptographic study; implementation comparisons do not prove complete security.

Paper Name: A Physical Hash for Preventing and Detecting Cyber-Physical Attacks in Additive Manufacturing Systems
University: Virginia Tech, Vanderbilt University School of Engineering
Attacks Mentioned: STL file manipulation, toolpath modification, process-parameter tampering, and intellectual property theft.
Defence Mentioned: Physical hash encoded as a QR code, combined with an air-gapped side-channel monitoring system for real-time verification of printing parameters and toolpaths.
Contribution: Proposes and experimentally validates a physical-hash approach that detects malicious modifications to STL files, process parameters, and toolpaths during material-extrusion printing.
Lifecycle stage: Protection of build specifications and verification during build execution.
Threat Model: Adversary alters the STL, toolpath or process parameters; defense assumes an air-gapped measurement system and trusted designer-specified hash and parameter ranges.
Purdue Stage: L3 geometry/toolpath preparation and hash specification; L0 printing, camera and physical QR code; L2 independent monitoring/inspection.
Paper Limitations: The proof of concept covers two attacks and selected monitored variables;

Paper Name: A review on machine learning in 3D printing: applications, potential, and challenges
Attacks Mentioned: Cybersecurity risks associated with AM and cloud-based manufacturing are included as a review topic;
Defence Mentioned: Reviews machine-learning applications relevant to cybersecurity and in-situ monitoring; does not propose or validate a new cybersecurity defense.
Contribution: Reviews ML techniques across AM design, material tuning, process optimization, in-situ monitoring, cloud services, and cybersecurity, identifying data acquisition, computational cost, and standardization challenges.
Lifecycle stage: Design and process optimization, manufacturing monitoring, and quality assessment.
Threat Model: Reviews machine-learning uses including attack detection for 3D printing; cited attacks
Purdue Stage: L3 design/optimization, L2 monitoring analytics, and L0 physical quality measurements;
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss limited datasets, model transferability, computing and standardization challenges

Paper Name: Assessing the Cybersecurity of Connected 3D Printers Using Large Language Models (LLMs)
Attacks Mentioned: Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks, malicious G-code modification, and unauthorized manipulation of printing instructions.
Defence Mentioned: LLM-based analysis of G-code to identify malicious instruction alterations and support potential real-time threat detection.
Contribution: Investigates cybersecurity vulnerabilities in connected 3D-printing workflows and explores LLMs as a method for detecting malicious G-code modifications.
Lifecycle stage: G-code preparation, transmission, and build execution.
Threat Model: Assumes adversary has network access and knows the printer IP, using ARP spoofing and packet capture to intercept and manipulate G-code between Cura host and Ultimaker S5.
Purdue Stage: L3 Cura/G-code preparation, L2 networked host/printer interface, L1–L0 printer execution and resulting part.
Paper Limitations: Authors report imperfect LLM error identification, including missed errors and false positives; reviewer observation: single testbed and investigated models do not establish general-purpose detection.

Paper Name: A Survey of Cybersecurity of Digital Manufacturing
University: New York University, Texas A&M University, College Station
Attacks Mentioned: IP theft, design and G-code tampering, reverse engineering, side-channel leakage, covert-channel attacks, denial-of-service, product sabotage, and counterfeiting.
Defence Mentioned: Dynamic watermarking, CAD obfuscation, embedded product-authentication codes, design fingerprinting, noise injection, anomaly detection, and IoT device-security measures.
Contribution: Develops a cybersecurity threat taxonomy for digital manufacturing, analyzes attack case studies, and reviews manufacturing-specific defenses across digital and physical systems.
Lifecycle stage: Digital authorization, design/toolpath preparation, manufacturing execution, and product authentication.
Threat Model: Digital-manufacturing survey discusses multiple adversary objectives and attack techniques; capabilities/access depend on cited cases rather than one new model.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 enterprise, L3 manufacturing engineering and L2–L0 control/physical equipment across surveyed workflows.
Paper Limitations: Broad survey spanning additive and subtractive manufacturing

Paper Name: A Survey on Limitation, Security and Privacy Issues on Additive Manufacturing
University: Colorado State University, Auburn University, University of Louisiana at Lafayette
Attacks Mentioned: Firmware manipulation, G-code tampering, side-channel IP theft, unauthorized printer access, design sabotage, sensor manipulation, material contamination, and equipment damage.
Defence Mentioned: Acoustic and sensor-based process verification, digital watermarking, authentication and access control, provenance mechanisms, and real-time attack monitoring.
Contribution: Surveys AM manufacturing limitations, cybersecurity threats, existing defense techniques, authentication frameworks, and security concerns across industrial applications.
Lifecycle stage: Access control and design protection, manufacturing execution, and verification of printed components.
Threat Model: Surveys diverse AM security/privacy attacks and authentication mechanisms;
Purdue Stage: L5 access/authentication and design exchange, L3 build preparation, L2–L0 device/control/physical process as discussed across cited cases.
Paper Limitations: arXiv preprint and narrative survey;

Paper Name: Attack-Defense Modeling of Material Extrusion Additive Manufacturing Systems
Where When Published: Critical Infrastructure Protection XVI (IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology, vol. 666); 2022
University: University of Tulsa, Johns Hopkins University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory
Attacks Mentioned: Cyberattacks targeting design, slicing, and printing processes; four case-study attacks involving identified system vulnerabilities and developed exploits.
Defence Mentioned: Attack-defense models identifying attack vectors, vulnerable components, and corresponding countermeasures for vulnerability mitigation.
Contribution: Develops phase-specific attack-defense models for material-extrusion AM and evaluates them through four attacks across three printers, ranging from hobbyist to industrial systems.
Lifecycle stage: Digital-design handling, slicing, and printing execution.
Threat Model: Attack-defense analysis models design, slicing and printing attack vectors and reports four attacks on three printers; attacker access/capabilities differ by case rather than one global adversary.
Purdue Stage: L3 design and slicing tools, L2 printer interfaces, L1 firmware/controllers and L0 printing process as affected by the specific case studies.
Paper Limitations: Three material-extrusion printer case studies and four attacks illustrate modeling, not a universal countermeasure effectiveness.

Paper Name: A Voxel-Based Watermarking Scheme for Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Unauthorized modification, copying, distribution, and reproduction of digital models, G-code, and printed objects; intellectual property infringement.
Defence Mentioned: Voxel-based digital watermarking using distance fields and self-organizing mapping (SOM), with watermark extraction and similarity-based authentication.
Contribution: Develops and experimentally evaluates a watermarking scheme that embeds signatures into geometric models, carries them into G-code and physical parts, and supports authentication of all three.
Lifecycle stage: Digital-model preparation, G-code generation and printing, and physical-part authentication.
Threat Model: Considers infringement and unauthorized copying of digital designs and printed parts; watermark decoding requires knowledge of the chosen encoding/view parameters, while a systematic adversarial removal trial is not established.
Purdue Stage: L3 voxel model watermarking and G-code preparation; L0 manufactured specimen and physical readout.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss noise introduced by G-code generation and fabrication and propose further volume-model tools; test examples do not establish robustness to all malicious removal.

Paper Name: BioSaFe: Bioprinting Security Framework for Detecting Sabotage Attacks on Printability and Cell Viability
Attacks Mentioned: Six sabotage attacks: nozzle switching, UV curing manipulation, thermodynamic/temperature manipulation, Z-profile (layer-height) manipulation, Quick Pause in Print (QPIP), and contamination through filtration-system manipulation.
Defence Mentioned: BioSaFe, an air-gapped, sensor-based monitoring framework comparing real-time process measurements with trusted G-code using spatiotemporal modeling.
Contribution: Introduces and experimentally evaluates six bioprinting sabotage attacks and a real-time detection framework on a CELLINK bioprinter, assessing impacts on printability and cell viability without requiring prior model training.
Lifecycle stage: Build execution, UV curing, and post-print quality assessment.
Threat Model: Assumes adversary can manipulate bioprinting parameters/process to sabotage printability or cell viability; monitoring compares measured behavior with trusted instructions. Exact initial compromise is not established here.
Purdue Stage: L3 trusted build instructions; L2 monitoring; L1 printer control; L0 sensors, extrusion and cell-bearing construct.
Paper Limitations: Experiments on an extrusion-based bioprinter and selected attacks/cell-quality metrics; generality across bioprinters is not established.

Paper Name: Blockchain-Based IoT Integration for VAT Photopolymerization Additive Manufacturing Process Security and Transparency
University: Marwadi University India, King Khalid University, Abha, Saudi Arabia
Attacks Mentioned: Potential unauthorized access, manipulation, and integrity compromise of IoT sensor data, particularly volatile organic compound (VOC) monitoring records. No specific cyberattack experimentally demonstrated.
Defence Mentioned: Private Hyperledger Fabric blockchain, AES-256 encryption, role-based access control, smart-contract validation, and automated safety alerts.
Contribution: Implements a blockchain-IoT framework for secure real-time monitoring of VOC emissions and environmental conditions during VAT photopolymerization, reporting 487.2 transactions/second and 99.99% data-integrity verification success.
Lifecycle stage: Manufacturing-process monitoring and traceable environmental compliance records.
Threat Model: Threats include unauthorized modification/access to IoT process/environment records; the paper does not establish a demonstrated attack or precise adversary access.
Purdue Stage: L0 VOC/environment sensors, L2 monitoring and L5 enterprise/blockchain access controls and records; deployment architecture is inferred.
Paper Limitations: Future work on multi-organization privacy, additional monitored variables, predictive control, and scalability/energy footprint. Environmental-record protection does not by itself establish protection of the physical print.

Paper Name: Blockchain-Based Quality Management for a Digital Additive Manufacturing Part Record
University: University of Rostock, Clausthal University of Technology, Germany
Attacks Mentioned: Potential tampering with manufacturing and quality records, unauthorized record modifications, and loss of data integrity or traceability. No experimental cyberattack demonstrated.
Defence Mentioned: Ethereum blockchain, smart contracts, decentralized data storage, and tamper-evident digital part records.
Contribution: Develops and demonstrates a blockchain-based digital part record for metal material-extrusion AM, supporting secure, transparent, and traceable quality documentation.
Lifecycle stage: Digital manufacturing records, production tracking, post-processing documentation, and quality assurance.
Threat Model: The paper motivates prevention of untraceable/unauthorized quality-record changes; a concrete attacker, capabilities and malicious trial are not established in the reviewed study.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 quality/part-record web application and decentralized storage; L0 manufacturing is the source of recorded data.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify data protection, network availability and usability as needing further work.

Paper Name: Blockchain-Based Traceability and Management for Additive Manufacturing
University: Khalifa University of Science and Technology, UAE, Birmingham City University
Attacks Mentioned: Man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks, replay attacks, unauthorized transactions, transaction tampering, and intellectual property/copyright infringement. No experimental attack demonstrated.
Defence Mentioned: Ethereum smart contracts, cryptographic transaction signatures, participant authorization, immutable transaction logs, and IPFS-based storage with blockchain-recorded hashes.
Contribution: Implements a blockchain-based AM supply-chain traceability system for spare parts, integrating design ownership, manufacturing transactions, product authentication, and certification. Includes smart-contract testing, security analysis, and transaction-cost evaluation.
Lifecycle stage: Order authorization, digital-design management, production tracking, and product certification.
Threat Model: Design owners, workshops and customers exchange designs and records; threat analysis considers unauthorized modification and replay, assuming protected participant private keys.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 enterprise smart-contract, design and certification records; L2–L0 workshop/sensor data are represented in the workflow.
Paper Limitations: Smart-contract tests and security/cost analysis do not validate truth of externally supplied records or every compromise of participant keys.

Paper Name: Characteristic Aspects of Additive Manufacturing Security From Security Awareness Perspectives
University: University of South Alabama, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Auburn University
Attacks Mentioned: Technical data/IP theft, spear-phishing, network session hijacking, side-channel information leakage, part sabotage, equipment damage, and unauthorized or illegal part manufacturing.
Defence Mentioned: NIST Risk Management Framework (RMF), cybersecurity risk assessment, security-control prioritization, and consideration of watermarking and unauthorized-print prevention techniques from existing research. No new technical defense experimentally evaluated.
Contribution: Analyzes AM security through three awareness perspectives: attack exposure, system security evaluation, and liability exposure. Compares AM with subtractive manufacturing to identify AM-specific security challenges.
Lifecycle stage: Digital-design protection, manufacturing security, post-processing concerns, inspection, and risk management.
Threat Model: Security-awareness analysis compares adversaries seeking technical-data theft, sabotage and illicit manufacture; attacker access and goals differ across reviewed scenarios.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 enterprise/data governance, L3 AM engineering, L2–L0 manufacturing and inspection, according to component discussed.

Paper Name: Comprehensive Threat Analysis in Additive Manufacturing Supply Chain: A Hybrid Qualitative and Quantitative Risk Assessment Framework
Attacks Mentioned: CAD/STL manipulation, IP theft, side-channel attacks, product-property sabotage, equipment manipulation, material contamination, and unauthorized access. Also considers non-adversarial operational, environmental, and financial risks.
Defence Mentioned: A hybrid qualitative–quantitative risk-assessment framework that prioritizes threats according to impact, likelihood, source reliability, and attack characteristics. Does not implement an attack-prevention mechanism.
Contribution: Identifies 22 AM-related risks across seven categories, develops a threat-ranking methodology, and validates its risk-assessment approach using the MITRE CVE dataset.
Lifecycle stage: Digital assets, manufacturing equipment, materials, production environment, and product integrity.
Threat Model: Prioritizes 22 literature-derived supply-chain threats using impact/likelihood characteristics and CVE data; threat actors and capabilities vary by risk and no single exploit is tested.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 supply-chain/organizational information, L3 engineering data and L2–L0 AM systems, depending on individual risk.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss limited post-processing coverage and need for further refinement; CVE-based analysis does not independently establish realized AM attack frequency.

Paper Name: Confidentiality Breach Through Acoustic Side-Channel in Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing Systems
Attacks Mentioned: Side-channel -> Acoustic attack
Contribution: Improvement of "Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks on Additive Manufacturing Systems"
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Acoustic eavesdropper places a recording device near the printer, models/trains stepper-motor acoustic features and infers G-code-related motion to reconstruct design IP
Purdue Stage: L0 printer acoustic emissions and physical movements revealing L1 machine-control behavior.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss dependence on sensor placement, distance and noise and suggest exploring multiple sensors; Learned inference and tested designs bound generalizability.

Paper Name: Cross-Domain Security of Cyber-Physical Systems: A Case Study on Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Kinetic Attack
Defence Mentioned:
* Intrusion detection systems
* Detection of Side-channel attacks
Contribution:
* Extention of "KCAD"
*  analyzing the relation between the cyber domain signals and the physical domain energy flows
Threat Model: Models a physical-to-cyber attacker recording acoustic emissions from a target 3D printer, with a similar printer used for model training, to infer G/M-code geometry; separately discusses kinetic attack detection. Initial access to the observation position is assumed.
Purdue Stage: L0 printer motors/acoustic emissions and physical print; L1 machine control; L3 G/M-code information being inferred. Framework's demonstration analyzes the source-to-output relation.
Paper Limitations: Paper reuses prior physical-to-cyber case results, with limited test objects/speeds; general framework examples do not establish security against all kinetic attacks or emissions.

Paper Name: Cyberattacks and Cybersecurity in Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Cyberattacks targeting CAD models, STL files, G-code/toolpaths, printers, sensors, actuators, and controllers; threats affecting the digital thread and physical supply chain.
Defence Mentioned: Authentication, digital watermarking, design obfuscation, cryptographic techniques, software integrity checks, anomaly detection, and process monitoring.
Contribution: Reviews cyberattacks, cybersecurity challenges, and existing countermeasures in AM, connecting AM security with Industry 4.0, IoT, industrial control systems, and digital manufacturing.
Lifecycle stage: Digital assets and authorization, build preparation, machine execution, and security monitoring.
Threat Model: Narrative survey covers CAD/STL/G-code theft or manipulation, firmware compromise, side-channel leakage and malicious material changes. The attacker identity, access and capabilities vary by cited study; it does not define a single adversary.
Purdue Stage: L5 CAD/file access; L3 slicing/toolpaths; L1 firmware/control and L0 printer/sensors
Paper Limitations: Survey discusses heterogeneous prior studies and countermeasures, without a common attack experiment or measured comparison;

Paper Name: Cyber-Attack Vectors Focused on Additive Manufacturing
University: University of Defence, Brno, Czech republic
Attacks Mentioned: Examines cyberattack vectors affecting additive manufacturing. The specific attack methods could not be reliably established from the accessible publication information.
Contribution: Investigates cyberattack vectors associated with AM. Detailed methodology and experimental findings require the full paper for verification.
Lifecycle stage: Build preparation and printer execution are relevant attack surfaces, but the paper's exact coverage remains unverified.
Threat Model: Assumes the attacker can edit exported G-code; demonstration manually changes extrusion and bed temperature on a Prusa i3 MK3S+. Phishing, compromised control PCs and network interfaces are discussed as possible routes, not demonstrated entry exploits.
Purdue Stage: L5 design/control workstation and discussed phishing; L3 exported G-code and slicer; L1 firmware execution; L0 extrusion and heated bed. Demo concerns L3 to L0 behavior.
Paper Limitations: Authors describe the demonstration as one of many possible malicious activities.

Paper Name: Cyber-Physical Attack Detection in Additive Manufacturing: An LSTM-Based Autoencoder Approach Using Reconstruction Error Analysis from Side-Channel Monitoring
University: Veltech Rangarajan Dr. Sagunthala R&D Institute of Science and Technology, Chennai, India
Attacks Mentioned: Cyber-physical attacks causing anomalous manufacturing-process behavior; specific attack manipulations could not be confirmed from the accessible publication material.
Defence Mentioned: LSTM-based autoencoder analyzing reconstruction errors in side-channel monitoring data to identify abnormal printing behavior.
Contribution: Presents a machine-learning-based approach for detecting cyber-physical anomalies in AM using side-channel signals and LSTM-autoencoder reconstruction-error analysis.
Lifecycle stage: In-situ monitoring and anomaly detection during printing.
Threat Model: Studies anomaly detection using accelerometer side-channel measurements and G-code-related process changes in a Prusa FFF setup. The paper does not specify a concrete adversary's initial access, attacker identity, or individual attack classes in sufficient detail.
Purdue Stage: L0 extruder/bed vibrations and accelerometers, L1 Arduino data acquisition, L2 processing/anomaly detection; L3 G-code changes provide context.
Paper Limitations: One desktop-printer setup; attack construction, dataset composition and splits are not sufficiently described. Numerical comparison in Table I and text is internally inconsistent, so performance should be treated cautiously.

Paper Name: Cyber-Physical Security Vulnerabilities Identification and Classification in Smart Manufacturing - A Defense-in-Depth Driven Framework and Taxonomy
University: University of South Carolina, University of Arizona
Attacks Mentioned: Product-geometry manipulation, internal-defect insertion, process sabotage, equipment compromise, data exfiltration, sensor tampering, and attacks evading production monitoring or quality inspection.
Defence Mentioned: Cyber-physical defense-in-depth integrating traditional cybersecurity, security-aware personnel, process monitoring, post-production inspection, and organizational security policies.
Contribution: Introduces a manufacturing-specific vulnerability taxonomy based on vulnerability–defense duality; demonstrates vulnerability identification, attack-chain mapping, and mitigation analysis using an illustrative manufacturing system and previously documented attack case studies.
Lifecycle stage: Digital-system security, process preparation and execution, monitoring, and inspection. Applicable to smart manufacturing broadly, not exclusively AM.
Threat Model: Illustrative MaaS case considers external actors accessing network/cloud to alter CAD or toolpaths and insiders with facility/data access stealing IP or sabotaging processes. Specific access is scenario-dependent; empirical AM examples are cited prior studies, not a new end-to-end attack.
Purdue Stage: Conceptual general-manufacturing L5 web portal/cloud and enterprise data, L3 planning and instructions, L2 supervision/monitoring, L1–L0 process and inspection. AM is discussed through prior examples
Paper Limitations: Framework and MaaS example are illustrative; empirical AM and CNC attacks are attributed to previous studies, not newly executed attacks.

Paper Name: Cyber-Physical Vulnerabilities in Additive Manufacturing Systems: A Case Study Attack on the .STL File with Human Subjects
Attacks Mentioned: altering .STL files
Defence Mentioned: Hashing/secure signing/blockchain
Lifecycle stage: Design -> Printing
Threat Model: Assumes an adversary can modify an STL design and insert internal voids to weaken a printed part while leaving exterior geometry unchanged. The study evaluates fabricated specimens and operator detection, not an actual cyber intrusion.
Purdue Stage: L5/L3 STL design handling, L3 preparation and slicing, L1–L0 printing/part formation, and L2–L0 inspection equipment.
Paper Limitations: Authors report human detection/diagnosis difficulties and propose physical hashing and improved monitoring as future work. Specific test specimen, subject population and controlled scenario do not establish detection behavior across production settings.

Paper Name: Cybersecurity Challenges for Manufacturing Systems 4.0: Assessment of the Business Impact Level
University: University of Salento, Politecnico di Bari, Bari, Italy
Attacks Mentioned: Analyzes potential external/insider breaches of manufacturing-data confidentiality, integrity and availability, including IP theft, altered design/process instructions and denial of service. These are assessed scenarios and literature examples, not newly executed cyberattacks.
Defence Mentioned: Applies four-step business-impact assessment: inventory critical data, identify consequences, map data to impacts and rank severity. It supports protection priorities; authentication, authorization and integrity checks are suggested examples, not tested technical controls.
Contribution: Studies CNC and powder-bed-fusion cells at one aeronautical manufacturer using focus groups, surveys and expert interviews. Links design, configuration, operating, machine-health and inspection data to business consequences through qualitative impact matrices. Company-specific judgments prioritize confidentiality and machine-setting data for AM, versus integrity and product-design data for CNC. These are perceived impacts, not measured losses or generalized attack probabilities.
Lifecycle stage: S1 design-information access; S2 build preparation, parameters and operation sequences; S3 execution telemetry and machine health; S5 workpiece inspection and corrective feedback. Coverage concerns data-risk assessment across these stages. Physical S4 postprocessing is not evaluated.
Threat Model: Potential insider/external actors compromise manufacturing-data confidentiality, integrity or availability, causing IP theft, changes or disruption. The assessment does not define a single attack chain or required attacker access.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 enterprise/business data and L3–L0 AM configuration, machine operation and inspection data; impact assessment spans these functions. Exact data-to-level assignments are contextual.
Paper Limitations: No live attack or measured defence effectiveness.

Paper Name: Cybersecurity for digital manufacturing
University: University of Central Florida, Pennsylvania State University, University of Nevada, Reno, University of Tennessee, Knoxville
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews unauthorized access, DoS, MitM, malware and data manipulation. Two AM scenarios concern unauthorized cloud-CAD geometry changes (bracket defects examined using finite-element analysis) and controller/program tampering that changes toolpath, units, temperature or feed rate; physical-access and compromised-host routes are discussed, not demonstrated as printer exploits.
Defence Mentioned: Reviews access control, encryption, authentication, intrusion detection and quantitative risk assessment. Discusses controller fuse/lock-bit configuration and protected bootloaders; recommends process monitoring and nondestructive inspection for embedded defects. These are reviewed/discussed controls, not a newly evaluated AM defence.
Contribution: Manufacturing-security review combining system characterization, threat/vulnerability pairs, attack scenarios, control families and risk-assessment methods; connects digital changes to physical product degradation.
Lifecycle stage: S1 design-asset access/authorization; S2 CAD-to-toolpath preparation and parameter manipulation; S3 controller access, firmware and build execution. S5 nondestructive inspection is a recommended defensive opportunity. No substantive S4 analysis identified.
Threat Model: Reviews multiple threats. Illustrative adversaries alter cloud CAD through account/host access or change controller programs via local or compromised-host access; the paper describes scenarios, not demonstrated intrusions.
Purdue Stage: L5 enterprise design/cloud access; L3 CAD/toolpath preparation; L1 controller and L0 printer; L2 monitoring and L0 inspection are discussed defences.
Paper Limitations: Broad review and hypothetical AM scenarios; no validation of the reviewed defence mechanisms.

Paper Name: Cybersecurity of Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems: A Review
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews industrial cyber/physical incidents and classifies sector, threat source, motivation, scope, domain, mechanism, active/passive type and affected CIA properties. Covers unauthorized access, malware and manipulation of control/sensor behavior; no AM-specific attack experiment is presented.
Defence Mentioned: Surveys countermeasures for common industrial weaknesses: boundary protection/DMZs, authentication, physical/access controls, logging, credential/account management, least privilege/functionality and secure remote access. Discusses edge anomaly detection, redundancy and resilient evaluation environments; these are reviewed approaches and research directions.
Contribution: ICPS security survey integrating industrial vulnerability reports, an adaptive multidimensional attack taxonomy, incident analysis, industrial protocol review and assessment of gaps in policy enforcement, datasets and testbeds.
Lifecycle stage: AM lifecycle stage not established. This industrial-control survey is contextual evidence; possible relevance to S3 control/monitoring; not an AM application studied in the paper.
Threat Model: Industrial CPS survey covering unauthorized access, malware and control/sensor manipulation across many attacker types. It does not define one AM-specific attacker or required access.
Purdue Stage: No AM-specific Purdue placement established. The industrial-control review is contextually relevant to monitoring and control functions; do not count as an AM-specific level assignment.
Paper Limitations: General industrial CPS review, not an AM-specific attack or defence evaluation.

Paper Name: Cybersecurity risks and mitigation strategies in additive manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews IP theft, design/STL corruption, malicious G-code or firmware, altered build orientation, and side-channel leakage. Examples of voids and mechanically weakened parts come from cited studies rather than new attacks.
Defence Mentioned: Proposes stage-by-stage vulnerability assessment and reviews physical-emission monitoring. Suggests encoding 3D design information through 2D images for encryption and comparison, but does not implement or cryptographically validate that proposal.
Contribution: Organizes AM threats around the digital-to-physical process chain and adapts manufacturing vulnerability metrics to its stages. Its contribution is a review and conceptual assessment framework, not measured detection performance or a demonstrated secure image-based protocol.
Lifecycle stage: S1 design/IP handling; S2 conversion/toolpath preparation; S3 printer/firmware operation. S4 finishing is named without a distinct safeguard. Final checking is a conceptual received-model comparison; operational S5 inspection is not demonstrated.
Threat Model: Reviews design/STL corruption, malicious G-code or firmware, IP theft and side-channel leakage; attacker access and capabilities vary by cited scenario and no single threat model is specified.
Purdue Stage: L3 design/build-file preparation; L1 firmware/control and L0 physical printer emissions. These represent reviewed functions, not a tested system architecture.
Paper Limitations: Narrative review and conceptual vulnerability framework; proposed image-encoding protection is not cryptographically validated.

Paper Name: Decoding Intellectual Property: Acoustic and Magnetic Side-Channel Attack on a 3D Printer
Where When Published: Security and Privacy in Cyber-Physical Systems and Smart Vehicles / Springer; 2025
University: University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Auburn University
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates passive IP theft: a nearby smartphone records acoustic and magnetic emissions while a printer operates; trained movement classifiers reconstruct G-code without modifying the printer.
Defence Mentioned: No countermeasure is implemented or evaluated. The paper characterizes side-channel exposure and discusses constraints relevant to later protection work.
Contribution: SCReG combines signal preprocessing and gradient-boosted decision trees for movement inference. A three-layer square is reconstructed with reported 4.47% mean tendency error at 15 cm; additional distance tests show degraded reconstruction. This is a limited proof of concept rather than validation on arbitrary complex parts.
Lifecycle stage: S3: emissions are captured during build execution; reconstructed toolpaths expose design IP. S4 and S5 are not studied.
Threat Model: Passive IP thief places a smartphone close to a running printer to record acoustic and magnetic emissions and infer G-code; no printer modification is required. Trained movement classifiers and nearby sensor access are assumed.
Purdue Stage: L0 physical printer emissions observed externally; disclosed information concerns process-control instructions at L1.
Paper Limitations: Limited proof of concept; accuracy and reconstruction degrade with distance and complex arbitrary parts are not established.

Paper Name: Detecting cyber-physical attacks in CyberManufacturing systems with machine learning methods
Attacks Mentioned: Models replacement of STL files with hidden infill voids and simulates five defect patterns. A separate CNC example modifies geometry or machining operation; it is not an AM attack experiment.
Defence Mentioned: Uses physical-data machine learning: grayscale image features with kNN, random forest, and anomaly detection for printing; acoustic features for milling. A printer camera prototype sends defect alerts to an operator.
Contribution: Combines simulated layer images and real MakerBot Replicator-2 images. AM anomaly-detection accuracy is 96.1% for the static camera but 72.5% for the moving camera, showing sensitivity to motion blur. The reported 91.1% average random-forest result belongs to CNC milling.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S2: malicious design substitution; S3: camera monitoring and alerts during printing. It detects introduced defects without independently proving malicious intent or implementing postprocessing security.
Threat Model: Simulated attacker replaces an STL with hidden infill voids; the AM tests assume access to substitute the file, not a demonstrated network compromise. A separate CNC example must not be treated as AM.
Purdue Stage: L3 model/toolpath preparation and L0 printer/camera observation; L2 supervisory alerting where used.
Paper Limitations: Controlled defect dataset and camera-position sensitivity; no end-to-end intrusion demonstrated.

Paper Name: Detecting Sabotage Attacks in Additive Manufacturing Using Actuator Power Signatures
University: University of South Alabama, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Auburn University
Attacks Mentioned:
*  Sabotage Attack
*
Defence Mentioned: side-channel intrusion detection method for additive manufacturing based on motor-current signatures
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Assumes model, host computer, communication network or printer can be compromised and used to sabotage a part; a trusted benign print produces a reference actuator-power signature. Initial compromise is assumed rather than the detector's demonstrated entry step.
Purdue Stage: L3 model and job transfer, L1 actuator control and L0 actuator power; independent power monitoring supports L2 process analysis.
Paper Limitations: Power signatures need a trusted baseline and monitored actuator channels; studied attacks and printer configurations do not prove coverage of every sabotage mechanism.

Paper Name: Digital Audio Signature for 3D Printing Integrity
Where When Published: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security; 2018
University: Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, University of South Alabama, Singapore University of Technology and Design
Attacks Mentioned:
* Sabotage Attack
* Side-channel attacks
Defence Mentioned: * Audio fingerprint verification
Contribution:
* propose an entirely new approach for generating and verifying the audio signature of a 3D printing process.
*
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Assumes original file/host/network/printer may be compromised to manipulate toolpath commands; a signed master acoustic fingerprint is generated from a verified benign reference print and compared against later stepper-motor audio.
Purdue Stage: L3 STL/G-code and trusted reference handling, L1 stepper control, L0 printer acoustics, and L2 independent audio-signature comparison.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify sensitivity to synchronization, recorder placement/device and same-length command replacements; transfer between printer types requires further calibration.

Paper Name: Digitally Twinned Additive Manufacturing: Detecting Flaws in Laser Powder Bed Fusion by Combining Thermal Simulations with In-situ Meltpool Sensor Data
University: University of Nebraska-Lincoln, Drexel University, SigmaLabs, Santa Fe, NM, United States, Navajo Technical University, NM
Attacks Mentioned: Emulates cyber sabotage by embedding internal spherical voids through selective laser suppression. Separate cases examine laser-power changes and lens delamination; these are induced flaw mechanisms, not demonstrated network intrusions.
Defence Mentioned: Combines in-situ meltpool/energy measurements with a graph-based thermal simulation and compares updated thermal histories against a nominal part to identify localized deviations.
Contribution: Tests four stainless-steel impellers built together on an EOS M290, with XCT and microstructural characterization corroborating flaws. Combining physics and sensor data distinguishes geometry-related thermal variation from process drift, planted voids and machine faults. Detection depends on model resolution and a nominal baseline; finer resolution costs computation. Results establish flaw detection in the tested build, rather than attribution of malicious intent or universal attack detection.
Lifecycle stage: S2 covers thermal-model preparation; S3 is the in-process detection focus. Post-build characterization validates the method and does not by itself establish operational S5 protection; S4 is not demonstrated.
Threat Model: Cyber-sabotage motivation: selective suppression of laser exposure emulates internal voids. The study induces defects and does not demonstrate an attacker or access path.
Purdue Stage: L3 thermal simulation, L2 in-situ monitoring, and L0 LPBF machine/meltpool; L0 physical XCT inspection supports evaluation.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify resolution/computation trade-offs and dependence on reference conditions; One build geometry/material and induced defects limit generalization.

Paper Name: Digital Twin and Cybersecurity in Additive Manufacturing
Where When Published: Journal of Cybersecurity Education, Research and Practice; 2024
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews AM threats including design/process tampering, sensor and network spoofing, denial of service, malicious software, and attacks on digital-twin data or models; no new adversarial experiment is performed.
Defence Mentioned: Surveys digital twins for monitoring and vulnerability assessment, alongside authentication, encryption, access control, machine learning, and blockchain. These are reviewed strategies, not a newly validated defence.
Contribution: Synthesizes AM digital-twin development, cyber digital twins, security challenges, and literature-derived case studies. The LPBF flaw-detection example, resilience-factor weights, and business-impact matrix reproduce cited research; they should not be attributed as new experiments.
Lifecycle stage: S1 design/data governance; S2 simulation/planning; S3 process monitoring/control. Table VI also reviews S4 postprocessing and S5 quality measurement within a lifecycle DT framework. These are literature coverage, not independently evaluated security at every stage.
Threat Model: Survey of data/model manipulation, spoofing, denial of service and theft across digital twins and AM; attacker privileges and access are case-specific and no new attacker experiment is defined.
Purdue Stage: Broad review spans L5–L4 data/management, L3 engineering and L2–L0 production and inspection; individual prior examples vary in scope.
Paper Limitations: Narrative review and secondary case studies; no original security defence evaluation.

Paper Name: Digital Twin-Based Cyber-Attack Detection Framework for Cyber-Physical Manufacturing Systems
Where When Published: IEEE Transactions on Automation Science and Engineering; 2024
University: University of Michigan, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD,
Attacks Mentioned: Simulates network attacks on a printer temperature-measurement stream using constant-offset and cyclic injections. These interfere with closed-loop heating control; fan cooling and degraded controller response serve as non-attack anomalies.
Defence Mentioned: A modular cybersecurity digital twin combines one-class SVM abnormality detection with signal-temporal-logic consistency monitoring to distinguish expected anomalies from suspicious inconsistencies. Human experts can investigate its reported predictions.
Contribution: Demonstrates the framework on an FFF printer with a networked controller. Robust detector variants improve discrimination, but some attacked intervals near setpoint changes are missed or classified as anomalies. The method identifies measurable effects rather than establishing malicious intent.
Lifecycle stage: S3: heating control, sensor-stream monitoring, and attack detection during printing. No postprocessing or product-certification mechanism is evaluated.
Threat Model: Models injected constant-offset and cyclic attacks against a networked temperature measurement stream. Attacker can alter that signal
Purdue Stage: L2 monitoring/digital twin; L1 controller and L0 temperature sensor/heating physical process.
Paper Limitations: Authors note specifications and historical/normal data are needed, and unseen anomalies may be confused with attacks

Paper Name: Digital Twins, AI, and Cybersecurity in Additive Manufacturing: A Comprehensive Review of Current Trends and Challenges
University: Missouri University of Science and Technology
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews hardware, firmware, network, data, and side-channel threats to AM, including sabotage and IP disclosure. Attack examples and performance results are drawn from earlier publications.
Defence Mentioned: Surveys conventional security controls, AI-based monitoring, digital twins, and blockchain. Proposes their integration with middleware into a closed-loop architecture for process checking, secure records, access control, and traceability.
Contribution: Synthesizes the intersection of digital twins, AI, and cybersecurity and identifies interoperability, data, cost, and computational challenges. The four-component framework is conceptual: no original implementation, attack campaign, or measured security validation establishes its claimed guarantees.
Lifecycle stage: S1 access/IP governance; S2 toolpath and parameter simulation; S3 monitoring/adaptive control; S5 proposed final-part authorization and quality-record traceability. These are reviewed/proposed functions; S4 protection is not separately demonstrated.
Threat Model: Reviews attacks on AM data, networks, firmware, hardware and side channels; cited threat models differ and the paper does not demonstrate an original attack.
Purdue Stage: Architecture spans L5–L4 data/access management, L3 preparation and L2–L0 monitoring and execution; placement is inferred from component functions.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify interoperability, data, cost and computation challenges; reviewer observation: proposed integrated AI/blockchain architecture is conceptual and not validated.

Paper Name: dr0wned: Cyber-Physical Attack with Additive Manufacturing
University: Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, University of South Alabama, Singapore University of Technology and Design
Attacks Mentioned:
*  Sabotage Attack
*
Defence Mentioned:
* use a classical applied cryptography solution, such as a digitally signed cryptographic hash of a digital design file
* Air-gapped communication with the printer
Contribution:

* Develop a sabotage attack against a specific 3D-printed quadcopter propeller, causing its mid-flight failure.
*
Lifecycle stage: Attack in Design flow
Threat Model: Adversary sends a malicious archive to a printer operator, compromises the control computer, modifies a propeller STL and seeks premature failure during drone flight. Access relies on victim interaction and a vulnerable desktop workflow; tested specific printer/drone and malicious design.
Purdue Stage: L5 user workstation/email and design files; L3 print preparation; L1–L0 print execution and physical propeller.

Paper Name: Dynamic-Thermal and Localized Filament-Kinetic Attacks on Fused Filament Fabrication Based 3D Printing Process
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates localized filament-kinetic and dynamic-thermal sabotage under compromised G-code/firmware. Retraction, extrusion-state or speed changes create internal defects; nozzle-temperature changes alter material properties while limiting visible or nozzle-motion changes.
Defence Mentioned: Discusses protected communications, firmware verification, access controls, and independent monitoring of filament kinetics and temperature. Coordinated space-time process analysis is proposed; a complete detector is not experimentally validated.
Contribution: PLA bar experiments on an Ultimaker-3 use tensile and bending tests to show that subtle extrusion and thermal changes affect mechanical performance. Keeping CAD/STL intact and much of the nozzle trajectory unchanged exposes limitations of design checks and motion-only monitoring.
Lifecycle stage: S2: malicious build instructions; S3: extrusion and thermal manipulation during execution. Mechanical testing evaluates attack effects rather than establishing S5 operational inspection.
Threat Model: Assumes compromised G-code or firmware enables targeted extrusion/retraction or nozzle-temperature changes to weaken internal material while minimizing visible changes. Initial compromise mechanism is not demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L3 G-code preparation, L1 firmware/control, and L0 extrusion and thermal physical process.
Paper Limitations: Attacker compromise assumed; mechanical tests cover specified PLA specimens and mitigations are not demonstrated.

Paper Name: Embedding of Taggants in the Vat Photo-Polymerisation Additive Manufacturing Process for Anti-Counterfeiting Measures
Attacks Mentioned: Targets counterfeit parts and physical copying of embedded identifiers, including an adversary possessing reference coordinates, color codes, and raw materials. Adversarial cloning is discussed rather than experimentally attempted.
Defence Mentioned: Embeds commercial color-coded taggants in VPP resin and combines optical identification with XCT-derived spatial information for a proposed physical/digital double lock. Coordinate binning and relative coordinates support later authentication.
Contribution: Demonstrates taggant incorporation, detection, distribution analysis, and thermal/mechanical characterization across layer thicknesses. The digital authentication workflow is proof of concept; the small quadrat code is explicitly unsuitable for commercial collision resistance, and cross-scanner and replication testing remain future work.
Lifecycle stage: S2: layer-thickness selection; S3: resin preparation and taggant embedding; S4: washing and UV/thermal post-curing; S5: optical/XCT enrollment and proposed customer authentication.
Threat Model: Counterfeiter aims to reproduce authenticated parts and may know reference coordinates, colour codes and raw materials; cloning is discussed, not experimentally attempted.
Purdue Stage: L0 physical incorporation of resin/taggants and XCT/optical inspection
Paper Limitations: Authors identify repeatability, scanner cost and limited small-code collision resistance

Paper Name: Embedding Tracking Codes in Additive Manufactured Parts for Product Authentication
Attacks Mentioned: Considers economically motivated counterfeiters with genuine parts and reverse-engineering capability, as well as unauthorized reproduction enabled by stolen design files. It does not demonstrate a network intrusion.
Defence Mentioned: Embeds segmented tracking codes at different internal depths so correct reconstruction requires appropriate viewing geometry. Micro-CT imaging and image processing recover the code for product authentication; segmentation also reduces structural disruption.
Contribution: Demonstrates embedded QR-code designs across polymer and metallic printing examples, imaging/reconstruction, and mechanical testing of resin specimens. Increasing segmentation provides obfuscation, but the study does not prove resistance to unlimited reverse engineering.
Lifecycle stage: Reviewer mapping: S1: code-bearing design creation; S2: segmentation and build parameters; S3: embedding during manufacture; S5: nondestructive reading for authentication. S4 is a compatibility limitation because heat treatment or hot isostatic pressing can destroy codes.
Threat Model: Counterfeiter can acquire genuine parts and attempt reverse engineering, or exploit stolen design files for unauthorized reproduction; no network intrusion is demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: Reviewer mapping: L3 embedded-code preparation; L0 printing, physical part and micro-CT inspection; L2 inspection workflow where applicable.
Paper Limitations: Reviewer observation: mechanical findings are specimen-specific and code survival/readability depend on process, resolution and postprocessing.

Paper Name: Encryption is Futile: Reconstructing 3D-Printed Models using the Power Side-Channel
University: Auburn University, Johns Hopkins University, University of Tennessee at Chattanooga
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates IP reconstruction by a malicious AM provider or insider who can instrument individual printer actuators. Current measurements reveal motor motion and extrusion even when customer files and communication remain encrypted.
Defence Mentioned: No physical-side-channel countermeasure is implemented. The paper discusses risk-management responses and explains why encryption-based DRM alone cannot protect against this physical-access adversary.
Contribution: Develops actuator-current interpretation and point-cloud reconstruction, evaluated on ten varied models printed on a Lulzbot Taz 6. Reported average distance-error bound is 0.79%; this is a motion-reconstruction metric, not proof of identical functional replicas. Reconstructed paths retain support material and reflect toolpath offsets.
Lifecycle stage: S1: outsourced manufacturing and IP exposure; S3: actuator instrumentation and observation during printing. Reconstruction is not an S5 product-inspection defence.
Threat Model: Malicious AM provider or insider with physical access instruments individual actuator currents to reconstruct customer geometry despite encrypted files/communications.
Purdue Stage: L0 motor current and physical emissions, exposing L1 actuator-control information.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss geometry reconstruction, support-material separation and printing limitations

Paper Name: Engineering Attack Vectors and Detecting Anomalies in Additive Manufacturing
Where When Published: Security and Privacy in Cyber-Physical Systems and Smart Vehicles, 2026
University: New Mexico Institute of Mining and Technology, Socorro, USA
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates host-root compromise and a rogue control interface enabling uploaded or live G-code manipulation, including extrusion changes, cavities, dimensional changes, and noise injection. Weak-password experiments use deliberately permissive lab configurations.
Defence Mentioned: Proposes log-based anomaly detection using transformer embeddings, contrastive representation learning, and an autoencoder trained on benign activity. Reconstruction errors distinguish manipulated behavior from normal printer logs.
Contribution: Evaluates attacks on Creality K1 Max and Ender-3 configurations and reports 95.37% overall log-sample classification accuracy. This establishes detection in the collected dataset, not comprehensive protection from a root attacker able to suppress or forge monitoring evidence.
Lifecycle stage: S2: file and parameter manipulation before release; S3: live control interference and log monitoring during execution. No operational postprocessing or certification mechanism is evaluated.
Threat Model: Host-root compromise and rogue interface allow attacker to upload/modify live G-code or change extrusion. Weak-password tests used deliberately permissive lab settings.
Purdue Stage: L3 job/G-code preparation; L2 printer host/control interface and logs; L1 controller and L0 physical process.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss structured log alignment and missed low-telemetry attacks; reviewer observation

Paper Name: Enhanced anti-counterfeiting measures for additive manufacturing: coupling lanthanide nanomaterial chemical signatures with blockchain technology
Attacks Mentioned: Addresses counterfeit printed parts and fraudulent digital provenance, including the possibility of compromised manufacturer credentials.
Defence Mentioned: Combines europium/terbium nanomaterial taggants in PLA with printed QR codes linked to Ethereum records. Smartphone measurements under controlled UV illumination compare fluorescence with ledger-stored reference values; ledger transactions also represent custody transfers.
Contribution: Demonstrates dual-extrusion printing of fluorescent QR features, stable emission signatures after processing, quantitative color measurement and actual metadata/custody transactions. The contribution connects a physical chemical signature to a digital part record. It is a proof of concept with manual ledger lookup, controlled imaging and protected private-key assumptions
Lifecycle stage: S1 covers recorded design/provenance information; S3 embeds taggants during printing; S5 covers post-production authenticity checks and custody verification. No finishing-stage S4 defence is shown.
Threat Model: Counterfeiters create fake printed parts or provenance and may compromise manufacturer credentials.
Purdue Stage: L0 taggants/part, UV and smartphone optical verification; L5 enterprise blockchain/provenance record.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify manual lookup, controlled imaging and private-key protection as practical constraints

Paper Name: Ensuring Additive Manufacturing Quality and Cyber–Physical Security via Side-Channel Measurements and Transmissions
Attacks Mentioned: Studies malicious alterations after trusted toolpath/signature creation: internal voids, changed infill settings and line-level extrusion edits. An altered design incorporated into the original reference signature would evade this premise.
Defence Mentioned: Embeds known-good process control limits into toolpath commands, transmitting them through printer motion to an air-gapped monitor. Independent position, extrusion and temperature measurements are checked against the decoded limits.
Contribution: Implements side-channel communication and monitoring on a material-extrusion testbed, detecting manipulated tensile bars and propellers, including a void representing 0.01% of propeller volume. The method accommodates natural process variation and avoids a network connection to the monitor. Repeated known-good prints are required to establish the signature, limiting suitability for one-off parts; the implemented transmission rate is slow.
Lifecycle stage: S2 covers signature generation and toolpath encoding; S3 covers physical transmission and build monitoring. No actual S4 intervention or operational S5 certification procedure is demonstrated.
Threat Model: Assumes trusted creation of baseline toolpath/signature; an attacker alters geometry, infill or extrusion commands afterwards. Corruption before signature creation is outside the detection premise.
Purdue Stage: L3 trusted job/signature creation; L1 toolpath/control commands; L0 motion/extrusion/temperature sensing with independent monitor.
Paper Limitations: Authors acknowledge trusted reference, repeated baseline prints and pre-signature attack limitation; Tested defect types do not establish universal detection.

Paper Name: Evaluation of a Cyber-Physical Attack Effectiveness in Metal Additive Manufacturing by Selectively Modifying Build Layer Thickness
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates metal-LPBF sabotage through build-design partitioning and zero core-laser exposure in selected internal layers while retaining contour scans. This emulates increased effective layer thickness without requiring compromised firmware.
Defence Mentioned: Recommends integrity protection for design/build files and rigorous inspection. X-ray tomography examines detectability; visibility depends on material and knowledge of the modified region, so the attack is not uniformly undetectable.
Contribution: Fabricates and tensile-tests stainless-steel specimens with one- and two-layer modifications on two LPBF systems. Mechanical degradation and defect visibility differ by material; larger modified thickness does not consistently cause worse ductility. The work lowers the assumed access barrier for process-parameter sabotage.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S2: design partitioning and exposure-parameter edits; S3: targeted unfused layers; S4: heat treatment of 17-4PH specimens; S5: X-ray inspection assesses detectability.
Threat Model: Sabotage is emulated through build design partitioning and suppressed internal core-laser exposure while retaining contours; ability to modify preparation/build specifications is assumed, not achieved through network intrusion.
Purdue Stage: L3 build preparation and laser-exposure instructions; L1 machine control; L0 LPBF and tomography inspection (CT Scan).
Paper Limitations: small specimens and tested materials/systems constrain generalization; no actual network intrusion.

Paper Name: Evaluation of Additive and Subtractive Manufacturing from the Security Perspective
Attacks Mentioned: Analyzes technical-data theft, sabotage, and illegal object manufacture across additive and subtractive manufacturing. Threat paths include compromised design/control data, software or firmware, physical materials, insiders, and power supply.
Defence Mentioned: Provides an attack-analysis framework linking access vectors, compromised elements, feasible manipulations, and adversarial effects. It supports identifying protection requirements; no new detector or preventive control is implemented or evaluated.
Contribution: Compares workflows to explain which risks transfer between manufacturing paradigms and which are AM-specific, particularly control over internal geometry and material microstructure. This is a conceptual security comparison supported by literature, not a new experimental attack demonstration.
Lifecycle stage: S1: designers, service relationships, and technical-data transfer; S2–S3: toolpaths, materials, and process control. S4 finishing and S5 nondestructive inspection are explicitly considered in the workflow, without validated stage-specific defences.
Threat Model: Qualitative threat analysis considers data theft, sabotage and illegal production via compromised design/control data, software/firmware, materials, insiders or power; capabilities depend on scenario.
Purdue Stage: L3 engineering/design preparation and L2–L0 manufacturing execution; broad AM/subtractive comparison, not a specific deployed architecture.
Paper Limitations: Qualitative generalized comparison; no original empirical security evaluation.

Paper Name: Firewall3D: A Hardware Firewall for Defending 3D Printers Against Firmware Attacks
Attacks Mentioned: Considers a compromised motherboard or firmware that alters motion, extrusion, thermal control, fans, or homing to sabotage parts, damage equipment, or facilitate leakage. Attacker control of the defensive hardware is excluded.
Defence Mentioned: Firewall3D independently monitors motor currents, temperature and fan signals, and endstop events against intended G-code behavior. Out-of-range or inconsistent behavior triggers an alert and can halt printing.
Contribution: Implements a separate hardware monitoring board and evaluates sensing accuracy plus representative motion, thermal/fan, and endstop attacks. The results support detection for tested physical-signal deviations, rather than protection against every firmware attack or passive IP side channel.
Lifecycle stage: S3: machine homing, actuator operation, heating/cooling, and execution-time detection. Installation requires physical wiring access
Threat Model: Assumes malicious printer motherboard/firmware controls motion, extrusion, thermal/fan and homing behavior; defender hardware and its trusted firmware are outside attacker control.
Purdue Stage: L2 supervisory PC/security channel, L1 independent hardware firewall and printer controller, L0 actuator/sensor signals and machine process.
Paper Limitations: Authors assume trusted firewall and communication channel; Threshold checks may miss attacks below detection sensitivity.

Paper Name: Fix the Leak! An Information Leakage Aware Secured Cyber-Physical Manufacturing System
Attacks Mentioned: Side-channel attacks
Defence Mentioned: * Leakage Aware G-Code generation
Contribution: * first work that demonstrates the idea of generating information leakage aware computer aided manufacturing tools for protecting the confidentiality of the manufacturing system.

Threat Model: Attacker observes acoustic, power or electromagnetic emissions from a running AM machine to infer G-code or design information; practical sensing access and physical positioning vary by scenario. The defense adjusts CAM-generated instructions.
Purdue Stage: L3 CAM/toolpath generation, L1 control outputs, L0 printer emissions. Mapping indicates leakage and mitigation locations
Paper Limitations: Conference-paper experiments concern a particular AM setup and side-channel models; reduced leakage is not proof of security against every sensor or inference algorithm.

Paper Name: FLAW3D: A Trojan-Based Cyber Attack on the Physical Outcomes of Additive Manufacturing
