Paper Name: Forensics of Thermal Side-Channel in Additive Manufacturing Systems
Attacks Mentioned: Investigates thermal side-channel IP leakage by recording a printer from within 95 cm and inferring nozzle/bed motion. The attack requires a camera view and prior knowledge of printer kinematics.
Defence Mentioned: No protective mechanism is implemented. The work analyzes leakage and proposes improvements to the attack sensing setup rather than validating a defence.
Contribution: Presents image processing, motion-to-speed mapping, and G-code reconstruction methods, with a polygon-print test on a Printrbot. Crucially, the report states the implemented attack did not meet its objective: single-view coverage, resolution, frame rate, and focus limitations prevented sufficiently accurate reconstruction. It is preliminary feasibility research, not demonstrated complete IP recovery.
Lifecycle stage: S3: thermal observation of build execution. The analysis reconstructs manufacturing information; it does not provide operational S5 authentication or forensics deployment.
Threat Model: Adversary records printer thermal emissions from a camera viewpoint within tested proximity and uses prior printer kinematics to infer motion and steal design information.
Purdue Stage: L0 thermal emissions and physical nozzle/bed motion, revealing aspects of L1 motion commands.
Paper Limitations: Authors report insufficient reconstruction accuracy and omit Z-axis movement in the tested setup; result is an unsuccessful reconstruction attempt, not a demonstrated full design theft.

Paper Name: FRoMEPP: Digital Forensic Readiness Framework for Material Extrusion Based 3D Printing Process
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes a knowledgeable adversary can compromise cyber components or firmware to sabotage extrusion printing. Demonstrated cases involve internal cavities, localized thermal changes, and timing manipulation; passive side-channel IP theft is excluded.
Defence Mentioned: FRoMEPP prepares for investigation by acquiring cyber logs and independent physical-process observations, standardizing and archiving them, and correlating evidence to printed objects through unique identifiers. It supports retrospective analysis rather than blocking attacks.
Contribution: Implements forensic readiness on an Ultimaker-3 and illustrates investigations of three sabotage cases using geometry, temperature, timing, printer, Cura, and network artifacts. Cross-domain correlation helps reconstruct manipulations and access paths; it does not guarantee attacker attribution from any single log.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S2: design, application, and build-file artifacts; S3: independent process monitoring and printer records; S5: post-incident investigation and feedback from failed parts. No S4 finishing security is demonstrated.
Threat Model: Assumes knowledgeable attacker compromises a cyber component or firmware to introduce cavities, thermal alterations or timing sabotage; passive side-channel IP theft is outside scope.
Purdue Stage: L2 forensic collection/logging, L1 firmware/controller and L0 extrusion and independent sensors; security correlation can include L3 job data.
Paper Limitations: Readiness infrastructure must be installed before incident; case study applies to material extrusion and selected sabotage scenarios.

Paper Name: Hiding My Real Self! Protecting Intellectual Property in 3D Printing Systems
University: Georgia Institute of Technology, Rutgers University
Attacks Mentioned: OPTICAL SIDE-CHANNEL ATTACK
Defence Mentioned: Side-channel ->  optical noise injection method
Contribution:
* propose an optical side-channel attack against 3D printers that enables adversaries to steal print designs through camera recordings during printing processes.
*  three novel noise generation algorithms to defend againts Side-channel Attacks
* used ResNet50, to recover the state-variable signal from the optical side-channel signal.
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Attacker obtains camera video of a 3D printer and uses learned image analysis to infer printhead trajectory/design. Defense analysis considers a stronger adversary aware of projected noise who trains on noisy images.
Purdue Stage: L0 printer movements and projected optical signals; L2 camera acquisition/monitoring; L3 inferred toolpath is the protected information asset.
Paper Limitations: Tested cameras, printer scenes and learned models bound the result; optical access is required and effectiveness against all adaptive attack strategies is not established.

Paper Name: How to Ensure Bad Quality in Metal Additive Manufacturing: In-Situ Infrared Thermography from the Security Perspective
University: University of South Alabama, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, CA
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes an adversary can manipulate IR thermography components or feedback. Analyzes calibration, camera, reference-data, shutter and control-loop tampering, which can distort laser control or mislead quality decisions; initial compromise is outside scope.
Defence Mentioned: Discusses limits of existing cyber and acoustic defences and the need for independent inspection.
Contribution: Builds an experimental pyrometer-based temperature loop and tests calibration changes, reduced loop frequency and false sensor signals. Laser weld tracks on a bare stainless-steel substrate show changed power response and track geometry.
Lifecycle stage: S3 covers compromised sensing and closed-loop processing. S5 quality decisions are analyzed for open-loop thermography, but not experimentally attacked in a qualification workflow. S4 consequences are discussed, without demonstrated intervention.
Threat Model: Assumes attacker access to IR thermography/feedback components can tamper with calibration, camera, reference data, shutter or control loops to affect quality and control; initial compromise unspecified.
Purdue Stage: L2 thermography/quality monitoring, L1 feedback control and L0 IR sensors and laser process.
Paper Limitations: Controlled powder-free weld tracks, not complete printed parts or measured mechanical strength; no protective mechanism validated.

Paper Name: Identifying 3D printer residual data via open-source documentation
University: University of South Alabama, Louisiana Tech University, Auburn University, The University of Texas at San Antonio
Attacks Mentioned: Identifies potential leakage of residual design/G-code data and tampering opportunities along removable-media and network transfer paths. These are inferred risks rather than newly executed attacks.
Defence Mentioned: Proposes forensic triage based on standalone capability and transfer methods, guiding investigators toward hosts, printer memory and intermediary media. Discusses encryption at rest, verifiable erasure and documented retention controls while recognizing investigation/privacy trade-offs.
Contribution: Surveys manufacturer documentation for 37 consumer-oriented printer models and develops two workflow classifications. Standalone operation and storage paths suggest where residual data may exist. The study analyzes documentation and supporting prior research; it does not acquire memory from all surveyed devices or verify recoverability experimentally. Documentation quality, historical model selection and a price cap restrict generalization.
Lifecycle stage: S2 covers slicing-host files and command transfer; S3 covers printer execution/storage. Incident forensics and privacy analysis are not equivalent to S5 product inspection; S4 is not established.
Threat Model: Considers residual-file disclosure and data tampering on printer media or network transfers. The paper infers possible access surfaces from documentation rather than demonstrating acquisition or attacks.
Purdue Stage: L3 build host and removable/job media; L2 printer interfaces/network transfer and L1 controller storage depending on device. Exact placement is model-dependent.
Paper Limitations: Documentation-based inference and historical consumer-printer sample; undocumented storage or capabilities can be missed.

Paper Name: Identifying Cyber-Physical Vulnerabilities in Additive Manufacturing Systems using a Systems Approach
Where When Published: 2020 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC); 2020
Attacks Mentioned: Analyzes technical-data theft through compromised networks/equipment, insiders, communication interception, side channels and equipment analysis. The case study selects these threats from prior literature rather than executing new attacks.
Defence Mentioned: Adapts Vulnerability Assessment and Mitigation matrices to connect architectural vulnerability attributes with fundamental countermeasures. It examines an existing acoustic-leakage defence and identifies supplementary controls, conflicting options and vulnerabilities introduced by mitigation.
Contribution: Provides a systems-level method for reasoning about interdependent AM security weaknesses. The worked example maps theft threats to physical, cyber and human attributes and candidate techniques. Recommendations rely on an existing judgment-based matching matrix and analyst choices; implementation and robustness testing of the proposed combinations are not performed, and the authors explicitly call for validation.
Lifecycle stage: S1 covers technical-data access and architectural security decisions; S3 includes exposure through manufacturing emissions. The analysis spans infrastructure conceptually, without demonstrating stage-specific S2, S4 or S5 protection.
Threat Model: Works through technical-data theft from communications, equipment, insiders and side channels using prior literature; no one access path or new intrusion demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 enterprise/communications context, L3 engineering information, L2–L1 printer/control interfaces and L0 acoustic emissions, depending on scenario.
Paper Limitations: Conceptual vulnerability-assessment example focused on technical-data theft; combined mitigations not experimentally validated.

Paper Name: Identifying the Cyber-Incidents in Additive Manufacturing Systems via Multimedia Signals
Where When Published: ASME International Symposium on Flexible Automation (ISFA 2020); 2020
Attacks Mentioned: Mimics sabotage by changing a cube’s internal infill from 100% to 50%, while considering broader upstream compromises that ultimately alter extruder motion. No initial cyber intrusion is implemented.
Defence Mentioned: Compares synchronized audio spectrograms with a benign reference using Wasserstein distance and a threshold. A second channel tracks a colored extruder marker in video to reconstruct paths for comparison with trusted G-code or benign recordings.
Contribution: Demonstrates detection on an Ender printer in a quiet laboratory using the first five minutes of recordings. Audio divergence identifies the manipulated run, while reconstructed paths visibly distinguish infill behavior. The evidence is a small case study, not a broad accuracy benchmark or industrial-noise robustness evaluation. Both channels depend on trustworthy references and motion-visible changes.
Lifecycle stage: S3 covers in-process audio/video monitoring; S2 G-code supplies an optional trusted comparison. No operational S4 intervention or S5 certification is demonstrated.
Threat Model: Emulates sabotage by changing cube infill from 100% to 50%; assumes a resulting modified print trajectory. Initial attacker access and cyber intrusion are not established.
Purdue Stage: L3 trusted G-code/reference, L2 monitoring, L1 motion commands and L0 extruder audio/video emissions.
Paper Limitations: One large infill change in a simple cube and quiet conditions; baseline trust/generalization are unestablished.

Paper Name: Implementing the Risk Management Framework for Additive Manufacturing Security: A Model-Based Approach
University: Stellenbosch University, Stellenbosch, South Africa, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD
Attacks Mentioned: Analyzes technological risks to LPBF product quality and intellectual property. An altered build file and scan strategy illustrate a threat/failure path; the paper does not execute an intrusion or sabotage attack.
Defence Mentioned: Applies model-based systems engineering to NIST RMF Prepare tasks, using system boundaries, information flows, and FMEA to derive and allocate security requirements, including verification of build files before use.
Contribution: Demonstrates traceable risk analysis for a commercial LPBF machine and its environment using SysML, IDEF0, and RAAML. The contribution is structured information and decision traceability, not completion of every RMF step or measured attack-detection effectiveness.
Lifecycle stage: S1: mission, assets, stakeholders, authorization and requirements; S2: build-file verification and preparation; S3: modeled machine, powder, and sensing flows. S4–S5 security controls are not independently validated.
Threat Model: Examines LPBF technological risks including a modified build file and scan strategy affecting quality/IP; attacker privileges and intrusion route are not demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L3 build file and scan-strategy engineering, L2 supervisory information flows and L1–L0 LPBF operation. Model-based RMF planning spans system boundaries.
Paper Limitations: Authors scope exercise to NIST RMF Prepare and technological risks; subsequent RMF activities are future work.

Paper Name: Implications of Malicious 3D Printer Firmware
University: University of South Alabama, Louisiana Tech University, Auburn University
Attacks Mentioned: Installs modified Marlin firmware on a Printrbot and triggers malicious behavior with a fan command. One version substitutes a pyramid for a requested cube; another increases extrusion while leaving incoming command validation intact.
Defence Mentioned: No protective mechanism is implemented. Missing host acknowledgments reveal the substitution demonstration, but extrusion manipulation retains normal logging. More sophisticated detection and forensic indicators are future work.
Contribution: Demonstrates that compromised firmware can bypass command-level checks by directly changing control variables. Increased extrusion produces visibly deformed prints, and the highest tested increase dislodges the part. The study is a physical proof of concept using USB commands; delivery of malicious firmware is excluded, and neither stealthy damage nor measured strength reduction is established. Detailed results distinguish the logging behaviors of the two attack variants.
Lifecycle stage: S3 is the core stage: firmware interprets commands and controls deposition. Printed-output inspection evaluates effects rather than establishing an operational S5 defence; S4 is not covered.
Threat Model: Assumes ability to install malicious printer firmware; hidden behavior is triggered by a fan command, substituting geometry or increasing extrusion while retaining normal logging in the latter case.
Purdue Stage: L1 printer firmware/controller and L0 extruder/printer process; L2 host acknowledgments/logs.
Paper Limitations: Installation is assumed, demonstrations are visible proof of concept; reported logging behavior differs between the two implementations.

Paper Name: Information Leakage-Aware Computer-Aided Cyber-Physical Manufacturing
Where When Published: IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security; 2018
Attacks Mentioned: Side-channel attacks
Defence Mentioned: * Leakage Aware G-Code generation
Contribution:
* Determining the design variables in cyber-domain (computer aided-manufacturing tools such as slicing and toolpath generation algorithm) that can be optimized to minimize the information leakage
* Leakage modeling and quantification for an additive manufacturing system
Lifecycle stage: Slicing -> Printing
Threat Model: Assumes adversary has unlimited access to a replica printer for supervised leakage-model training and can observe physical side-channel emissions to infer G/M-code; leakage-aware CAM changes orientation and speed to reduce information exposure.
Purdue Stage: L3 CAM slicing/toolpath/orientation selection, L1 machine control, and L0 acoustic/power/magnetic/vibration emissions from the physical FDM printer.
Paper Limitations: Authors use a Cartesian FDM printer and benchmark models; optimal parameter choices trade printing time against leakage. Reduction in measured mutual information or a tested attack success rate is not a guarantee against every sensor or reconstruction model.

Paper Name: Intellectual Property Protection in Additive Layer Manufacturing: Requirements for Secure Outsourcing
Where When Published: Proceedings of the 4th Program Protection and Reverse Engineering Workshop; 2014
Attacks Mentioned: Considers malicious designers, process-tuning experts, manufacturers and external adversaries stealing geometry/process IP, bypassing production licenses, intercepting transfers or reverse engineering parts and emissions.
Defence Mentioned: Derives prevention, attribution and forensic requirements. Proposes restricted information disclosure, encrypted manufacturing specifications with trusted hardware/key management, watermarking and residual-data analysis as research directions, while recognizing untrusted manufacturers’ physical access.
Contribution: Introduces an outsourcing model separating object design, manufacturing-parameter expertise and production. Its risk assessment treats both geometry and tuned process knowledge as licensable IP and identifies trust conflicts among participants. The contribution is a requirements and research framework; secure key handling, license enforcement, watermark robustness and forensic tools are not implemented or experimentally validated.
Lifecycle stage: S1 covers licensing and cross-party access; S2 covers process-parameter specification; S3 covers protected execution and side-channel risks. Attribution of manufactured objects is a proposed downstream function, not a demonstrated S5 inspection workflow; S4 is not established.
Threat Model: Considers dishonest designers, tuning experts, manufacturers and outsiders seeking geometry/process IP or unlicensed production via transfer interception, reverse engineering and physical emissions; capabilities vary by role.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 outsourcing/authorization, L3 engineering/process data, and L0 physical parts/emissions; reviewed access paths do not imply an implemented architecture.
Paper Limitations: Conceptual requirements and proposals, with no implemented/evaluated cryptographic, watermarking or forensic system.

Paper Name: KCAD: Kinetic Cyber-Attack Detection Method for Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing Systems
Attacks Mentioned: Kinetic Attack
Defence Mentioned:
* Intrusion detection systems
* Detection of Kinetic Attack
Contribution:
* attack detection method that is able to detect zero-day kinetic cyber-attacks on AM by identifying anomalous analog emissions
* Detecting the intrusion/attack that can occur at various points of the digital process chain of AM
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Attacker can alter CAD, slicing or firmware information flow, changing machine control parameters to create physical defects. Evaluation implements firmware changes to motion speed, axis and distance; initial compromise is assumed.
Purdue Stage: L5 CAD/design and L3 slicing/instructions, L1 printer firmware/control and L0 acoustic emissions/physical motions; L2 independent KCAD analysis.
Paper Limitations: Initial compromise is assumed. Authors state the method is machine-specific and requires training; experiments use simple firmware-driven motion variations, with more complex attacks and printer variation left for future work.

Paper Name: Layered Security Guidance for Data Asset Management in Additive Manufacturing
Where When Published: Journal of Computing and Information Science in Engineering, 24(7); 2024
University: National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews AM data theft, sabotage, and unauthorized manufacture to motivate risk-based guidance. Design-to-toolpath conversions and data relationships create opportunities for malicious geometry or parameter changes; no new attack is executed.
Defence Mentioned: Layers AM-specific asset-management guidance onto existing IT/OT guidance using the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. OSCAL catalogs and profiles encode composable modifications and traceable publication workflows.
Contribution: Develops an asset-management example centered on mapping organizational communication and data flows, relating geometry and process definitions, and automating guidance composition. It provides a structured method for maintaining security guidance rather than a deployed manufacturing detector or experimentally validated control.
Lifecycle stage: S1: governance, responsibilities, and data assets; S2: geometry/process definitions and format conversion; S3: machine/process data relationships. Postproduction is contextual, with no distinct S4 or S5 intervention demonstrated.
Threat Model: AM guidance considers data theft, sabotage and unauthorized manufacture. Data conversion and dependencies create manipulation opportunities; no single attacker or new attack is implemented.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 data management and governance, L3 engineering assets and L2–L0 production data assets; layered guidance spans rather than validates a specific deployment.
Paper Limitations: Guidance construction and one asset-management example, not demonstrated attack detection or mitigation effectiveness.

Paper Name: Leave Your Phone at the Door: Side Channels that Reveal Factory Floor Secrets
Where When Published: Proceedings of the 2016 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security; 2016
University: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, Advanced Digital Sciences Center, Singapore
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates phone-based acoustic and magnetic leakage from a 3D printer and CNC mill, allowing reconstruction of manufacturing outlines. A reference-signature library, knowledge of operating conditions, domain constraints, and human assistance support inference.
Defence Mentioned: Tests playback of similar manufacturing sounds as obfuscation, but remaining harmonics still permit reconstruction. Suggests motor shielding and increased separation/enclosures; these are recommendations with limited validation rather than a complete proven defence.
Contribution: Builds an interactive reconstruction framework and reconstructs previously unseen printed outlines. Experiments assess phone sensor quality, distance, machine signatures, and geometric errors. Magnetic usefulness falls sharply with distance, and manual segmentation contributes length error.
Lifecycle stage: S3: emissions are recorded during manufacturing and converted into design/process information.
Threat Model: Phone-equipped adversary gathers acoustic/magnetic emissions near a 3D printer or CNC mill, aided by calibrated reference signatures, operating knowledge and human segmentation, to infer outlines.
Purdue Stage: L0 physical machine emissions revealing L1 movement/control behavior; phone is external observer.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss limited sensor range, manual segmentation and remaining harmonics despite sound obfuscation;

Paper Name: Leveraging Memory Forensics to Investigate and Detect Illegal 3D Printing Activities
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates a local-root attacker modifying G-code during Cura/CuraEngine inter-process communication, including thermal, cooling, and layer-height changes. Illegal-printing investigations motivate artifact recovery, but suspicious files alone do not establish intent.
Defence Mentioned: SliceSnap uses Volatility 3 plugins and Python-object analysis to recover Cura meshes, G-code, settings, metadata, and logs. G-parser compares recovered instructions with settings to flag discrepancies.
Contribution: Evaluates recovery across models and Cura/Python configurations, reporting complete extraction in controlled tests, and detects demonstrated parameter manipulations. Artifact availability changes across slicing stages; removal or modification of scene objects can clear G-code references. No illicit objects were physically printed.
Lifecycle stage: S2: slicing-memory acquisition and manipulation detection; S3: downstream printing effects.
Threat Model: Adversary with local root access changes G-code in Cura/CuraEngine inter-process communication; forensic investigators recover volatile artifacts to detect inconsistent settings and support investigation.
Purdue Stage: L3 slicer host, in-memory geometry, settings and G-code; evaluated manipulation happens before physical execution.
Paper Limitations: Authors note artifact recovery depends on slicing stage and object references; Tested Cura configurations and recovered anomalies cannot alone establish criminal intent.

Paper Name: Low-Magnitude Infill Structure Manipulation Attacks on Fused Filament Fabrication 3D Printers
Attacks Mentioned: An insider intercepts an unencrypted printer connection using ARP poisoning and alters G-code coordinates. Two attacks increase infill-line or vertex spacing to create internal weak regions while compensating motion/material totals. Low-magnitude changes target the tolerance of monitoring schemes.
Defence Mentioned: Micro-CT inspection reveals selected attacked internal structures. Proposed countermeasures include authenticated/encrypted printer links, firmware checks, physical-property-aware monitoring and automated in-process imaging; no deployed real-time detector is evaluated.
Contribution: Demonstrates both attacks on solid-filled PLA tensile bars, using dimensional inspection, microscopy, selected micro-CT scans and tensile testing. Small coordinate changes can reduce strength, but the smallest changes have limited effects and larger defects become easier to observe. Claims about evading existing monitors rely on their reported resolution, rather than comprehensive detector testing.
Lifecycle stage: S2 covers G-code integrity before execution; S3 covers altered internal deposition; S5 covers evaluated micro-CT inspection. No operational S4 intervention is established.
Threat Model: Insider with access to an unencrypted printer connection uses ARP poisoning to intercept and alter G-code coordinates, subtly weakening infill while controlling aggregate motion/material changes.
Purdue Stage: L2 host/printer communications, L1 controller commands and L0 printed infill and micro-CT inspection; source G-code originates at L3.
Paper Limitations: Solid-filled PLA specimens and selected scans; no exhaustive experimental evasion of other monitoring systems.

Paper Name: Machine Learning-Based Early Detection of Malicious G-code Manipulations in 3D Printing
Attacks Mentioned: Studies malicious filament-flow, thermal-control and Z-profile changes embedded in G-code, including cavities, extrusion-state changes, fan or temperature changes, and layer-height manipulation.
Defence Mentioned: Engineers G-code features for attention-based bidirectional LSTM layer detection and random-forest/MLP command detection before printing, without a separate reference model for each part. Command-level models address subtle changes that the layer model can miss.
Contribution: Evaluates generated benign and attacked files drawn from 600 generated G-code files with a held-out test split, and reports physical face-shield and drone case studies. Random forests perform better for several subtle thermal/Z manipulations. The evaluation supports preprint screening of represented attack families; it does not establish reliable detection of every unseen attack. Small X/Y deviations and multiple attacks within a layer or command remain limitations.
Lifecycle stage: S2 is the defensive focus through preprint instruction analysis; S3 appears in physical attack demonstrations. S4 and operational S5 coverage are not established.
Threat Model: Adversary modifies preprint G-code to manipulate flow, temperature, fan or layer height. The evaluation studies generated attack files rather than establishing an initial compromise route.
Purdue Stage: L3 build-file preparation and G-code screening; L1 commands and L0 physical print case studies.
Paper Limitations: Authors state limitations for small XY deviations and multiple attacks in one command/layer; Synthetic manipulations limit unseen-attack generalization.

Paper Name: Machine Learning-Based Investigation of the 3D Printer Cooling Effect on Print Quality in Fused Filament Fabrication: A Cybersecurity Perspective
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes a remote adversary can change cooling-fan settings during fused-filament fabrication, potentially degrading the surface quality of a printed part.
Defence Mentioned: The FSAD OctoPrint plugin predicts roughness from layer thickness, infill density and fan speed using a neural network. It checks queued fan commands against an initial-quality threshold, warns for quality-preserving changes and rejects predicted harmful changes.
Contribution: Prints 135 parameter/shape combinations and measures surface roughness, using clustering to define quality thresholds and comparing regression with neural-network prediction. The neural network has lower prediction errors and is deployed through TensorFlow Lite on a Raspberry Pi with a Prusa printer. This demonstrates a quality-based command guard; the paper does not establish general intrusion-detection accuracy or distinguish adversarial intent from every legitimate parameter adjustment.
Lifecycle stage: S2 covers parameter/model preparation; S3 covers checking cooling commands during printing. Roughness measurements support development and evaluation, without establishing an operational S5 inspection defence.
Threat Model: Assumes a remote adversary can manipulate cooling-fan settings, affecting print surface quality. The work does not demonstrate the initial network exploit.
Purdue Stage: L2 OctoPrint host/plugin, L1 fan commands and L0 printer/fan and surface inspection.
Paper Limitations: Authors limit deployed support to PrusaSlicer G-code; Surface roughness is a quality proxy and an intrusion campaign was not evaluated.

Paper Name: Manipulation of G-code Toolpath Files in 3D Printers
University: Johns Hopkins University, University of Tulsa, Oak Ridge National Laboratory
Attacks Mentioned: With root access to a local slicing host, an attacker scans the running slicer’s heap, reconstructs ASCII G-code fragments and overwrites equal-length bytes. Demonstrated changes lower selected-layer temperature or omit infill while preserving plausible toolpath files.
Defence Mentioned: Recommends stronger access control, signed/encrypted updates, obfuscating in-memory G-code and detecting suspicious memory scanning. These mitigations are proposals, not evaluated defensive implementations.
Contribution: Implements attacks against two unnamed open-source slicers. Printed specimens show approximately 14% tensile-strength reduction for the temperature attack and 10.6% or 19.9% compressive-strength reduction for two infill-exclusion settings. Recoverability differs substantially between slicers. The method depends on readable dynamic G-code copies and constrained byte replacement; limited external changes do not establish evasion of all inspection methods.
Lifecycle stage: S2 is the compromise point inside the slicer; S3 executes the malicious thermal and deposition instructions. Mechanical tests evaluate consequences and do not alone establish S5 coverage; S4 is not demonstrated.
Threat Model: Attacker with local root access scans a slicer heap and overwrites readable ASCII G-code fragments using equal-length substitutions to change temperature or omit infill.
Purdue Stage: L3 slicer host and in-memory G-code; L1 controller instructions and L0 printed specimen effects.
Paper Limitations: Authors describe dependence on readable in-memory G-code and constrained byte replacement;

Paper Name: Manufacturing and Security Challenges in 3D Printing
University: New York University Tandon School of Engineering, New York University Abu Dhabi, University of Texas at Dallas
Attacks Mentioned: Malicious and deliberate modification of the print orientation
Contribution: More reguarding print evaluation and understanding print errors
Lifecycle stage: Design -> Slicing -> Printing
Threat Model: Considers malicious alteration of print orientation or embedded defects that can weaken a part; experiments assess modified specimens. Specific attacker identity and digital entry route are not demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L3 build orientation/design inputs, L1–L0 fabrication and L2–L0 ultrasonic/material inspection. Attribution of edits to a real cyber intrusion is not established.
Paper Limitations: Authors note an embedded defect was undetectable by their ultrasonic test and did not reduce measured tensile strength, although stress concentration may matter elsewhere.

Paper Name: Materials vs digits: A review of embedded anti-counterfeiting fingerprints in three-dimensional printing
Where When Published: Materials Science and Engineering: R: Reports; 2024
University: University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, China
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews counterfeiting and unauthorized reproduction enabled by stolen designs, copied material formulations or reverse engineering of printed objects. It introduces no new cyberattack experiment.
Defence Mentioned: Surveys material-response fingerprints, including optical/spectral/deformation features, alongside intrinsic printer signatures and artificial digital watermarks, codes and radio-frequency tags. Proposes combining material and digital features with practical verification methods.
Contribution: Organizes prior authentication research by security feature, forming process, material and readout method. The review highlights printing-resolution limits, material compatibility, structural-strength trade-offs and expensive/nonportable inspection. Integrated multi-feature schemes and smartphone-readable authentication are research directions rather than a newly validated universal solution.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S2 include designing/encoding authentication features; S3 embeds or generates them; S5 verifies provenance/authenticity. S4 finishing and heat treatment are discussed as feature-survival constraints, without a newly evaluated postprocessing defence.
Threat Model: Surveys counterfeiting via stolen designs, copied material formulations and reverse engineering of parts. Individual attacks and required access vary across cited literature; no original adversarial trial.
Purdue Stage: L3 digital watermark/model creation and L0 physical taggants, printed-part authentication and measurement; exact components vary across studies.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify resolution, compatibility, strength trade-offs and inspection costs; {roposed cross-feature integration and low-cost verification are research directions.

Paper Name: MitM Attacks on Intellectual Property and Integrity of Additive Manufacturing Systems: A Security Analysis
University: Jordan University of Science and Technology, Irbid, Jordan, The University of Tennessee at Chattanooga
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates LAN man-in-the-middle attacks on a Stratasys Dimension Elite: stealing transmitted proprietary CMB models, substituting another model and replacing internal part material with support material. ARP poisoning and a protocol-aware proxy enable interception.
Defence Mentioned: Recommends stronger communication/integrity protection and encryption. No defence is implemented or tested; ordinary checksums are insufficient because the manipulated file can be repacked with a valid checksum.
Contribution: Reverse engineers CMB handling, supplies parsing/visualization tools and physically validates interception, substitution and internal-material tampering. Four compression specimens show changed mechanical response despite similar exterior appearance. The sabotaged specimens require more force at selected displacements and exhibit different deformation/fragility; these results should not be summarized as a demonstrated percentage strength reduction. Scope is one printer/software/network setup.
Lifecycle stage: S2 covers transfer and integrity of prepared toolpaths; S3 realizes material substitutions during fabrication. Compression testing evaluates consequences rather than constituting an operational S5 defence;
Threat Model: LAN attacker uses ARP poisoning and a protocol-aware proxy to intercept a Stratasys workflow, steal CMB models, substitute jobs or replace internal build material.
Purdue Stage: L2 networked host/printer interface, L1 machine/control job execution and L0 resulting physical part; L3 design file is affected.
Paper Limitations: One proprietary printer/software setup and limited physical specimens; mechanical response is not reducible to a universal strength-decrease claim.

Paper Name: Model-Based Security Analysis in Additive Manufacturing Systems
Where When Published: ACM CCS Workshop on Additive Manufacturing Security (AMSec@CCS); 2022
Attacks Mentioned: Models potential confidentiality, integrity and availability failures in a representative modified laser-AM architecture, including vulnerable I/O and controller paths.
Defence Mentioned: Uses AADL/OSATE and VERDICT architectural analysis to generate attack/defence evidence, identify failed requirements and recommend CAPEC-linked NIST controls. Updating modeled defence strengths satisfies the illustrative requirements; synthesis compares relative defence costs.
Contribution: Demonstrates a reproducible modeling workflow and security-assurance-case output for a Concept Laser M2-derived research architecture. The paper explicitly presents a research illustration, not a cybersecurity audit of a particular machine. Results depend on model annotations and assurance assumptions; behavioral formal verification and comprehensive return-on-investment analysis are future work. Relative cost units are not measured monetary savings.
Lifecycle stage: Modeled assets span S2 part-description transfer and S3 controller/laser operation; analysis occurs before deployment. No operational S4 or S5 workflow is evaluated.
Threat Model: Models potential CIA violations through modeled I/O and controller vulnerabilities in a representative laser-AM architecture
Purdue Stage: L3 engineering/security modeling, L2 supervisory interfaces, L1 modeled controllers and L0 physical process. Assignments are functional model interpretations.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify future behavioral verification and comprehensive ROI analysis; Architectural illustration rather than specific-machine audit or deployed control test.

Paper Name: Modeling of smart additive manufacturing processes for attack analysis and detection
Where When Published: 2025 33rd Euromicro International Conference on Parallel, Distributed, and Network-Based Processing (PDP); 2025
University: Research Laboratory of Computer Security Problems St. Petersburg Federal Research Center of the Russian Academy of Sciences (SPC RAS), Saint Petersburg, Russian Federation
Attacks Mentioned: Simulates USB-path model theft and instruction tampering in a PC-controlled printer workflow. The altered model removes internal layer content while retaining outer contours; initial network compromise is not experimentally established.
Defence Mentioned: Reconstructs transmitted G-code from captured USB request traffic and compares it with the original model to expose modifications. Timing/statistical indicators for passive theft detection and richer sensor/learning methods are proposed without quantitative detection validation.
Contribution: Builds a BQ Prusa i3 Hephestos 2 testbench, records print traffic and implements Python/Scapy recovery of model commands. Examples visualize original and modified layer content and demonstrate information exposure through USB captures. Current recording occurs on the control PC; the authors recommend printer-side capture to observe modifications occurring between endpoints. Strength degradation is inferred rather than measured mechanically.
Lifecycle stage: S2 covers prepared instructions and transfer integrity; S3 covers printer communication and execution observations. No S4 intervention or operational S5 part-certification process is established.
Threat Model: Simulates a USB-path adversary who can intercept printer traffic and steal models or tamper with instructions. Initial PC/network compromise is not established.
Purdue Stage: L3 PC/job preparation and recovered G-code, L2 host-to-printer communications, L1 printer control and L0 printed geometry.
Paper Limitations: Authors note current host-side recording cannot observe all between-endpoint changes; Small laboratory simulation and theft detection has no quantified performance.

Paper Name: Multi-Modal Attack Detection for Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Considers compromised firmware that changes printer actions while the reference G-code remains trusted and unmodified. Corruption upstream of that trusted reference is outside this detection premise.
Defence Mentioned: Uses acoustic, vibration, magnetic and current measurements to infer printer control states with supervised models, then compares the inferred states with expected G-code behavior. Multiple physical channels provide corroborating observations.
Contribution: This short overview summarizes the authors’ multimodal monitoring approach and related evaluation on an Ultimaker 3. The reported 98.15% accuracy comes from synthetic attacks constructed by pairing modified G-code with original sensor traces. Two physical wrench/gear demonstrations also show detection of deliberately visible alterations; these examples do not establish performance against every concealed defect or unseen attack.
Lifecycle stage: S3 covers sensing build execution and detecting firmware-induced control deviations.
Threat Model: Assumes compromised printer firmware alters actuator behavior while original G-code is trusted. An attacker who modifies the reference before comparison is outside this premise.
Purdue Stage: L3 trusted G-code reference; L1 printer firmware/control; L0 acoustic, magnetic, vibration and current signals; L2 monitoring analysis.
Paper Limitations: Headline accuracy uses synthetic attacks and trusted reference assumption limits coverage.

Paper Name: Needle in a Haystack: Detecting Subtle Malicious Edits to Additive Manufacturing G-code Files
University: New York City College of Technology, Vellore Institute of Technology, Indian Institute of Technology Goa, National Institute of Technology Surathkal, New York University Abu Dhabi, New York University

Defence Mentioned: * Side-channel detection
Contribution: Automatically detecting defects in g-code

Paper Name: Never Trust the Manufacturer, Never Trust the Client: A Novel Method for Streaming STL Files for Secure Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Addresses design theft and unauthorized reproduction by a manufacturer, alongside potentially harmful G-code supplied by a client. These are motivating threats; the prototype evaluation does not demonstrate a comprehensive adversarial security test.
Defence Mentioned: Streams horizontal STL sections over a secure channel for local manufacturer-side slicing, execution and deletion. Client-generated supports and alignment guides enable section-wise processing; buffering reduces pauses. Security assumes protected controller memory and a secure printer connection.
Contribution: Implements printing of a gear, a supported complex object and tensile specimens. Streaming produces comparable geometry and modest observed load differences in the tested samples. However, the authors acknowledge that a manufacturer retaining successive slices can reconstruct the full design. Consequently, the approach limits routine exposure under its assumptions rather than establishing confidentiality against an unrestricted malicious manufacturer.
Lifecycle stage: S1 covers controlled design disclosure; S2 covers section generation and local slicing; S3 covers streamed execution. Tensile experiments do not establish operational S5 coverage, and S4 is not demonstrated.
Threat Model: Considers a potentially dishonest manufacturer seeking the full client design and a client supplying harmful G-code. Protection assumes secure printer connection and protected memory, while manufacturer may retain slices.
Purdue Stage: L5 client/manufacturer transfer, L3 STL sectioning/local slicing and L1–L0 printer control/execution.
Paper Limitations: Authors acknowledge accumulated slices can reconstruct the whole design; Assumed memory/link security limit the confidentiality claim.

Paper Name: Obfuscation of Embedded Codes in Additive Manufactured Components for Product Authentication
University: Tandon School of Engineering, New York University
Attacks Mentioned: Addresses unauthorized reproduction from stolen design files or reverse-engineered parts. Counterfeiter effort is discussed, but an adversarial reverse-engineering trial is not performed.
Defence Mentioned: Embeds segmented, interpenetrating authentic and decoy QR codes in CAD. Feature dimensions and slicing orientation determine which code survives fabrication; internal imaging or optical viewing then supports product authentication.
Contribution: Demonstrates orientation-dependent code production in material-extrusion polymer parts read by micro-CT and transparent material-jetted parts inspected optically. Obfuscation links correct processing settings to the intended code, without proving that a determined adversary cannot reproduce it. Resolution, slice thickness, viewing/readout quality and defects constrain performance. Mechanical effects are discussed rather than systematically tested, and metal printing or post-treatment survival is not validated.
Lifecycle stage: S1 covers protected code design; S2 controls slicing/orientation; S3 produces the embedded features; S5 reads them for authentication. The authors explicitly leave S4 postprocessing effects unstudied.
Threat Model: Counterfeiter may obtain design files or reverse-engineer physical parts to reproduce authenticators; paper does not experimentally attack the authentication scheme.
Purdue Stage: L3 CAD code embedding and slicing/orientation; L0 polymer printing, optical/micro-CT inspection and physical part.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss resolution and readout constraints; No measured adversarial resistance, mechanical campaign or postprocessing validation.

Paper Name: Offensive and Defensive Perspectives in Additive Manufacturing Security
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews AM threats including intellectual-property theft through files or side channels, geometry/parameter/firmware sabotage, and illegal part manufacture. Prior attacks are organized using STRIDE and by adversary intent, rather than introduced as new experiments.
Defence Mentioned: Compiles NIST-derived recommendations covering authentication and access control, protected logging, network boundaries, secure communications, vulnerability management and trusted system components. These are organized by threat category; their effectiveness is not experimentally evaluated in the paper.
Contribution: Provides a structured survey linking published attacks, research purposes and defensive guidance. It identifies gaps in repudiation coverage, evidence about manufacturers’ security practices, AM-specific attack opportunities and controls against harmful fabrication. The authors explicitly caution that one vulnerable consumer-printer case cannot establish industry-wide insecurity.
Lifecycle stage: S1 includes design access and IP protection; S2 includes file and preparation integrity; S3 includes firmware, process manipulation and emissions.
Threat Model: Survey of prior threats including IP theft and sabotage; STRIDE organizes threats, rather than specifying a single attacker. Access and capabilities differ by cited study; no unified operational adversary is specified.
Purdue Stage: L5 enterprise design/file access; L3 preparation files; L1–L0 printer firmware, process and emissions. Conceptual survey;
Paper Limitations: Authors identify limited evidence about actual manufacturers' practices and gaps in some threat categories. Reviewed attacks and recommended controls; a single vulnerable printer case does not establish industry-wide insecurity.

Paper Name: Offramps: An FPGA-Based Intermediary for Analysis and Modification of Additive Manufacturing Control Systems
Where When Published: 2024 54th Annual IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks (DSN); 2024
University: New York University; New York University Abu Dhabi; University of New South Wales
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates hardware interposition that changes motor, extrusion, heater, and fan control signals, enabling part alteration, denial of service, or equipment damage. Separately emulates firmware-style extrusion reduction and material relocation through modified G-code.
Defence Mentioned: OFFRAMPS captures STEP/DIR pulse counts after firmware execution and compares them with a trusted reference. All eight tested Flaw3D-style cases were detected; this detector does not cover heater manipulation.
Contribution: Introduces an open-source FPGA intermediary between Arduino/Marlin and RAMPS, providing a common platform for controlled attack injection and execution monitoring. Its nine illustrative hardware Trojans and separate detection experiment establish experimental capabilities rather than universal protection.
Lifecycle stage: S3: machine control, attack injection, and in-process monitoring. Trusted G-code/reference preparation supports S2; no actual finishing or certification workflow is evaluated.
Threat Model: Adversary can physically interpose programmable hardware between controller and RAMPS and modify motor/heater/fan signals; aims include part sabotage, denial of service or equipment damage. Detector assumes a trusted reference and host link.
Purdue Stage: L1 local controller/STEP-DIR signals and L0 actuators/physical print; L2 measurement/reference monitoring. L3 trusted G-code provides reference context.
Paper Limitations: Authors report their detector does not cover heater manipulation or undervolting. Tests use a RAMPS/Marlin setup and require trusted reference and host communication;

Paper Name: On Cyber Sabotage Risks in Automated Manufacturing of Advanced Composites
Attacks Mentioned: Analyzes sabotage of automated fibre placement through altered geometry, ply trajectories, process parameters and autoclave recipes. A phishing/USB-propagation narrative illustrates a possible attack chain and is explicitly fictional, not an executed intrusion.
Defence Mentioned: Suggests independent physical monitoring, restricted/encrypted data transfer, access control, updates, logging, software assurance and attacker-informed risk management. Warns that quality monitoring can trust corrupted designs or replayed sensor data; proposed protections are not experimentally evaluated.
Contribution: Applies an AM attack-analysis framework to the documented UNSW composite-manufacturing workflow, connecting compromised components, feasible manipulations, mechanical consequences and detectability. It extends threat reasoning beyond layup to curing and distinguishes remotely accessible digital parameters from manipulations requiring physical access. The contribution is workflow-grounded risk analysis and a research agenda, not measured sabotage or defence performance.
Lifecycle stage: S1 includes design access; S2 includes layup planning/simulation; S3 includes robot execution and sensing; S4 explicitly includes post-layup autoclave curing. S5 nondestructive inspection appears as a future defensive direction.
Threat Model: Conceptual outsider/insider scenarios assume varying digital access to geometry, layup plans and process settings, or physical access for some manipulations, seeking defective composite parts. Phishing/USB infection is fictional; no live intrusion demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L5 design access; L3 layup planning and simulation; L1–L0 robotic layup and autoclave operation; L2 supervision/monitoring. These are analysis targets, not observed compromise.
Paper Limitations: Workflow-based qualitative analysis and fictional scenario; no new sabotage or defence experiments.

Paper Name: One Video to Steal Them All: 3D-Printing IP Theft through Optical Side-Channels
University: Georgia Institute of Technology, University of Texas San Antonio
Attacks Mentioned: An adversary obtains a monitoring-camera recording and reconstructs printable G-code without knowing the target instructions or object placement. The assumed video shows the whole printer; camera compromise is an entry assumption, not a demonstrated exploit.
Defence Mentioned: Discusses camera patching, firewall/access controls, and possible software verification alternatives. Reusing reconstruction to detect malicious toolpaths is a proposed extension requiring further evaluation, not a validated defense.
Contribution: Combines learned video-to-nozzle-trajectory inference with extrusion/speed postprocessing and a rotation/translation-invariant curve checker. Evaluation includes recorded printing datasets and functional counterfeit key/gear demonstrations; trajectory similarity does not establish equivalent structural integrity.
Lifecycle stage: S3: optical leakage during printing and reconstruction from monitoring footage; the stolen G-code also exposes S2 manufacturing instructions.
Threat Model: Attacker obtains video of a whole operating printer through a monitoring camera and seeks G-code/design reconstruction. No target instructions or object-position knowledge assumed; camera compromise is assumed, not demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L0 printer movements observed optically; L2 camera monitoring and video; L3 manufacturing instructions are inferred targets. Mapping describes observation and exposed asset, not demonstrated network entry.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss constrained camera/data conditions and reconstruction metric limitations. Matching shape does not establish equal quality or strength.

Paper Name: Online Detection of Cyber-Incidents in Additive Manufacturing Systems via Analyzing Multimedia Signals
Attacks Mentioned: Mimics sabotage by reducing internal infill while preserving the external shape of an FDM cube. The experiment changes printing conditions directly rather than demonstrating an intrusion; additional attack signals and smaller infill changes are simulated.
Defence Mentioned: Uses Wasserstein-distance monitoring of audio spectra and Hausdorff-distance comparison of camera-reconstructed nozzle paths. Audio needs a trusted benign trace; video can use trusted G-code. These are separate detection approaches, with sensor fusion left for future work.
Contribution: Ender-printer experiments compare distance metrics and demonstrate online detection of substantial infill reduction. Sensitivity deteriorates for smaller simulated changes; acoustic noise, camera obstruction and sensor placement constrain performance. Detection establishes process deviation, not malicious intent.
Lifecycle stage: S3: in-process acoustic and visual monitoring. S2 G-code supplies a trusted reference;
Threat Model: Hypothetical sabotage changes infill while preserving external geometry; experiments directly print altered conditions, not an intrusion. Detection assumes a trusted benign audio trace or trusted G-code; attacker access route and capabilities are not demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L0 printing emissions and movements; L2 camera/audio monitoring; L3 trusted G-code reference
Paper Limitations: Authors note audio noise and camera obstruction and reduced sensitivity for small changes. One printer, two recorded attack traces and simulated smaller changes; trusted reference integrity is assumed.

Paper Name: Operational Resilience of Additively Manufactured Parts to Stealthy Cyberphysical Attacks Using Geometric and Process Digital Twins
University: Rutgers University, University of Connecticut, University of Texas at El Paso, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, University of Michigan
Attacks Mentioned: Emulates stealthy attacks by removing geometric features and changing printing parameters or filament material. These introduce geometric errors, inter-line voids or overprinting; network infiltration is outside the experiments.
Defence Mentioned: Geo-DT compares physics fields against trusted customer-supplied fields and uses topology optimization to recover geometry. Pro-DT combines in-situ imaging with a pretrained reinforcement-learning controller that adjusts feed rate and stage speed without retraining for tested unknown disturbances.
Contribution: Demonstrates geometric recovery in simulation and defect disruption in an FFF testbed, including selected untrained temperature, nozzle-height and material changes. Secure execution and trustworthy reference fields are assumed. Complex toolpaths, other defect classes and other AM processes remain open; suppressing new defects does not itself establish complete restoration of part strength.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S2: verification and recovery of digital geometry before fabrication. S3: sensing and adaptive process correction during printing
Threat Model: Threats include malicious geometry changes or process/material changes intended to introduce defects. Experiments emulate disturbances without demonstrating network entry; recovery relies on trusted customer reference fields and assumed secure execution.
Purdue Stage: L3 geometry verification/recovery and process preparation; L2 in-process sensing and adaptive supervisory response; L1–L0 motion/process control and physical printing.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify limited defect classes and need to extend to complex toolpaths and other AM processes. Geometry recovery is simulated; measured defect reduction does not prove full strength recovery.

Paper Name: Power Consumption-Based Detection of Sabotage Attacks in Additive Manufacturing
University: University of South Alabama, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Singapore University of Technology and Design
Attacks Mentioned:
*  Sabotage Attack
*
Defence Mentioned: continuous monitoring of the current delivered to all actuators during the manufacturing process and detection of deviations from a provable benign process
Contribution: * novel approach for detecting sabotage attacks
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Attacker can manipulate a printer process to sabotage part quality; detector monitors current supplied to actuators and compares against a provably benign reference process.
Purdue Stage: L1 actuator control and L0 actuator power; L2 independent current monitoring. Build instruction reference context is L3 when present.
Paper Limitations: Outcomes for tested X/Y changes do not establish detection of every possible manipulation.

Paper Name: Practitioner Paper: Decoding Intellectual Property: Acoustic and Magnetic Side-channel Attack on a 3D Printer
Attacks Mentioned: A nearby smartphone records acoustic and magnetic emissions from stepper-driven printing. Supervised models infer nozzle movements and reconstruct G-code, threatening design confidentiality without touching or modifying the printer.
Defence Mentioned: Discusses encryption, watermarking, and blockchain protection from prior work, but implements or evaluates no countermeasure. Its physical-emissions attack motivates stronger IP protection.
Contribution: Combines acoustic and magnetic features with Gradient Boosted Decision Trees, then reconstructs instructions and tests a physical object. Reported movement classification and reconstruction errors are distinct metrics; distance, background noise, fast movement, and similar motor loads limit inference.
Lifecycle stage: S3: passive observation of the active printer; recovered instructions expose S2 toolpaths. S1 outsourcing/IP access provides context, with no implemented authorization mechanism or S4/S5 intervention.
Threat Model: Nearby adversary records printer acoustic and magnetic emissions using a smartphone, then applies trained models to infer motion and reconstruct toolpath/design; no physical modification or access to print files is required.
Purdue Stage: L0 stepper motors and physical emissions; L1 motor-control-driven motion; L3 reconstructed manufacturing instructions as the targeted information asset.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss distance, background noise, fast movements and similar motor loads as challenges. limited objects and close-range smartphone setup;

Paper Name: Protecting Additive Manufacturing Information When Encryption Is Insufficient
Where When Published: ASTM STP 1644: Progress in Additive Manufacturing 2021; 2022
Attacks Mentioned: Analyzes an outsourced-AM scenario in which an insider obtains proprietary geometry through a printer power side channel despite encryption at rest and in transit. The technical attack is drawn from prior research, not newly demonstrated.
Defence Mentioned: Applies the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, SP 800-171, and SP 800-53 to identify risk assessment and external-system-use controls. Suggested safeguards include restricted physical access, surveillance, employee awareness, contractual conditions, provider verification, or retaining sensitive production in-house.
Contribution: Provides a worked risk-management interpretation connecting generic security guidance to AM threat taxonomies, customer priorities, and trust in a service provider. It argues that selecting appropriate organizational controls is essential when encryption cannot stop physical leakage.
Lifecycle stage: S1: supplier selection, authorization, contracting, and risk planning; S3: provider-site access controls address printing emissions.
Threat Model: Outsourced production scenario considers a provider insider who observes printer power and infers proprietary geometry despite encryption in storage and transit. Trust in the service provider and physical access are central assumptions; attack drawn from prior research.
Purdue Stage: L5 supplier contracting and enterprise data protection; L0 printer power/physical emissions in provider facility. L3 design or instruction files are the protected information, not an evaluated compromise.
Paper Limitations: Worked on conceptual scenario with no measured control effectiveness. Results depend on provider conduct and do not newly demonstrate the referenced attack.

Paper Name: QuietPrint: Protecting 3D Printers Against Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks
Where When Published: Proceedings of the 12th ACM Cyber-Physical System Security Workshop; 2026
Attacks Mentioned: Studies acoustic reconstruction by a recording device near an FDM printer, using motor direction-change spikes and cooling-fan sound to infer movement. The demonstrated reconstruction uses controlled toolpaths and known motion assumptions.
Defence Mentioned: QuietPrint rewrites G-code with nonprinting Stealth Head Movement extensions, making leaked movement resemble an enclosing shape. An optimization trades added travel against shape dissimilarity; reconstruction and transition-prediction experiments test obfuscation.
Contribution: Provides a software-only acoustic confidentiality defense and examines two emission sources. Printed examples demonstrate altered reconstructed shapes, while the key example incurs substantial extra printing time. Results establish feasibility on the studied printer and attack method, not resistance to every acoustic or multimodal adversary.
Lifecycle stage: S2: modifies prepared G-code; S3: executes additional movements to obscure printing emissions.
Threat Model: An adversary positions an audio recorder near an FDM printer and infers movement from motor and cooling-fan sounds to reconstruct geometry. Analysis uses controlled toolpaths and stated motion assumptions.
Purdue Stage: L3 G-code rewriting to add decoy travel; L1–L0 motor control and motion emissions during printing. The mapping indicates defense implementation and leakage locations.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss limited reconstruction setup and runtime overhead. evaluation does not establish resilience to every acoustic or multimodal adversary.

Paper Name: Real-time Process Authentication for Additive Manufacturing Processes based on In-situ Video Analysis
University: Mississippi State University, The University of Texas at Arlington
Attacks Mentioned: Represents sabotage through altered internal geometry and infill orientation in FFF parts. These modifications are deliberately fabricated for detector evaluation; no network or firmware compromise is implemented.
Defence Mentioned: An extruder-mounted microscope continuously captures texture. Adaptive segmentation filters low-information regions; layer-wise distributions of orientation and feature length form tensors. Multilinear PCA and Hotelling T-squared charts flag departures from a nominal printed reference.
Contribution: Four PLA specimens on a Prusa i3 MK3S support a small demonstration: one nominal training part, one nominal test part and two altered parts. Selected layer statistics separate the tested cases without error. Sensitivity, broader geometry and infill coverage, and attack diagnosis remain future work; the result is not a general detection guarantee.
Lifecycle stage: S3: layer-wise authentication during printing, responding to S2 geometry or toolpath alterations.
Threat Model: Detection study emulates sabotage by fabricating parts with altered geometry or infill; compromise method and attacker access are not demonstrated. A trusted nominal print/reference baseline is assumed.
Purdue Stage: L0 printing and microscope observations; L2 image capture and in-process monitoring; L3 reference build configuration.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify sensitivity, wider geometry/infill coverage and attack diagnosis as future work. Four PLA specimens, nominal baseline and final 20-layer evaluation; printed group labels are inconsistent.

Paper Name: Review, Meta-Taxonomy, and Use Cases of Cyberattack Taxonomies of Manufacturing Cybersecurity Threat Attributes and Countermeasures
University: University of South Carolina, University of Arizona
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews manufacturing attacks by method, target/location, and consequence, covering sabotage, information theft, and attacks on digital and physical production assets. These are synthesized prior threats, not newly executed attacks.
Defence Mentioned: Organizes published countermeasures and proposes linking controls to deployment location, threat type, and response strategy. Risk assessment, attack-graph reasoning, and implementation of cybersecurity frameworks are illustrated uses rather than validated protective systems.
Contribution: Builds a meta-taxonomy from existing manufacturing taxonomies and identifies missing threat actors, system vulnerabilities, physical deviations, countermeasure coverage, and relationships among attributes. It proposes ontology-based knowledge representation and explains how taxonomies could support security-tool development.
Lifecycle stage: Broad manufacturing review with AM design-file, build-instruction and production side-channel examples relevant to S1–S3.
Threat Model: Manufacturing-security taxonomy survey covers sabotage and IP theft with varied attacker access and objectives from prior works
Purdue Stage: General manufacturing taxonomy with examples involving enterprise design, engineering instructions and process/control functions; potential relevance across levels. No AM-specific deployment or precise assignment at every level established.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify missing attributes and relationships in published taxonomies. no deployed AM defense is empirically validated.

Paper Name: Sabotage Attack Detection for Additive Manufacturing Systems
Attacks Mentioned:
