*
Defence Mentioned:
Side-channel detection:
acoustic, magnetic, vibration, and power
Contribution: * novel multi-modal sabotage attack detection system
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Models adversaries modifying CAD/CAM software, control computers or printer firmware to alter object information and sabotage parts; illustrative infection routes are prior incidents, not newly demonstrated intrusions. Detection relies on independent side-channel sensing and original G-code-derived controls.
Purdue Stage: L5 CAD/workstation, L3 G-code/CAM processing, L1 firmware/control parameters, L0 analog sensor emissions, and L2 multimodal inference/detection.
Paper Limitations: Authors report challenges with short curved segments, small coordinated changes across parameters and testing on one printer model.

Paper Name: Sabotaging Material Extrusion-Based 3D Printed Parts Through Low-Magnitude Kinetic Manipulation Attacks
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates network man-in-the-middle modification of G-code to weaken infill-line, infill-vertex, infill-to-wall, or interlayer bonding through small kinetic deviations. Attacks target mechanical properties while keeping external dimensions and mass apparently normal.
Defence Mentioned: Evaluates evasion of the existing Sophos monitor: outcomes depend on attack type and magnitude. Discusses network authentication/encryption and firmware integrity controls; exploratory micro-CT detects some larger defects but manual examination misses subtle changes and is difficult to scale.
Contribution: Connects printer tolerance windows with process-specific sabotage opportunities, using PLA tensile/flexure specimens, mechanical tests, and a defense-evasion case study. It demonstrates that small, visually inconspicuous movements can change strength; effects vary by attack and loading direction.
Lifecycle stage: S2/S3: tampered instructions and physical build execution. S5 appears in exploratory post-build micro-CT detection; destructive strength testing primarily validates attack impact.
Threat Model: Network man-in-the-middle adversary can modify G-code in transit and subtly alter infill/interlayer bonding, seeking strength degradation without obvious dimensional or mass changes. The tested monitor's trust assumptions bound its evasion assessment.
Purdue Stage: L3 build instructions and transfer; L1 controller interprets modified instructions; L0 printer motions and part bonding. L2 Sophos monitoring and L0/2 micro-CT inspection are evaluated defenses.
Paper Limitations: Authors test selected kinetic magnitudes and discuss evasion/inspection limits.

Paper Name: Sabotaging Metal Additive Manufacturing: Powder Delivery System Manipulation and Material-Dependent Effects
University: University of South Alabama, Auburn University, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, CA
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes an already-compromised powder-bed-fusion machine and analyzes powder-delivery manipulations that create layer, thermal, timing, or kinetic defects. Experiments simulate a selected layer-thickness attack through modified build specifications, rather than demonstrating initial machine compromise.
Defence Mentioned: Tests visual inspection, microscopy, and micro-CT for attack detection; detectability varies with material and defect geometry. These are assessed inspection methods, not a new validated cyber-defense.
Contribution: Develops a structured analysis of individual and compound powder-delivery manipulations and evaluates fatigue effects in 17-4PH and 316L stainless-steel specimens. Results show material-dependent damage and inspection limitations; not every proposed manipulation is experimentally tested.
Lifecycle stage: S2/S3: altered build specifications and powder-layer execution; S5: inspection-evasion evaluation.
Threat Model: Assumes a powder-bed-fusion machine is already compromised; attacker modifies powder delivery or effective layer thickness to create defects and degrade fatigue performance. The experiment modifies build specifications; initial access is not demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L3 modified build specifications; L1–L0 powder-layer actuation and metal fabrication; L2–L0 inspection instruments and analysis. Compromise path to controller is assumed, not demonstrated.
Paper Limitations: Controlled specimens and different material/machine pairings limit generalization; not all analyzed manipulations are tested.

Paper Name: SCREAM: Secure Channels for Real-time Evaluation of Additive Manufacturing
Where When Published: Proceedings of the 21st ACM Asia Conference on Computer and Communications Security (ASIA CCS); 2026
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes attackers can alter host software, transmitted G-code, firmware or bootloader while the defender retains a trusted STL. Evaluations reproduce material reduction, relocation and internal-hole effects, without demonstrating every original compromise mechanism.
Defence Mentioned: SCREAM directly taps STEP/DIR signals for motion and extrusion, reconstructs executed G-code with tickCollector, and compares aggregate metrics and layers against supplied instructions and the trusted model. Final model checking includes visual comparison, rather than an entirely automated geometric proof.
Contribution: Combines pulse simulation with RAMPS1.4/Marlin printer measurements to recover toolpaths and identify selected manipulations, including extrusion changes. Pulse commands provide hardware-observable evidence but do not establish actual material deposition or temperature integrity. Sampling rate, physical access and device calibration constrain deployment.
Lifecycle stage: S3: runtime actuation monitoring. S1 trusted design and S2 instructions provide references; finishing and finished-part certification are not tested.
Threat Model: Attacker may modify host, G-code, firmware or bootloader to alter print geometry or material; defender has trusted STL and can physically tap motor signals. Some attacks are recreated through modified G-code, not deployed firmware malware.
Purdue Stage: L3 trusted model and instructions; L1 STEP/DIR controller signals; L0 actuators; L2 external reconstruction/monitoring. Pulse evidence is not direct measurement of deposited material.
Paper Limitations: Authors note sampling/calibration and hardware constraints. Hot-end temperature excluded, tested board/printer configuration limited

Paper Name: SECUREAM: Advancing Cybersecurity in IoT-Enabled Additive Manufacturing
Where When Published: 2025 12th International Conference on Internet of Things: Systems, Management and Security (IOTSMS); 2025
University: University of Southern Denmark, Odense, Denmark
Attacks Mentioned: Identifies IP theft, data manipulation, production disruption and sabotage as risks in interconnected AM supply chains. This project description presents no executed attack or measured adversarial case.
Defence Mentioned: Plans a two-stage approach: threat and risk assessment followed by an architecture combining blockchain auditability with secure multiparty computation for confidential collaboration.
Contribution: Defines SECUREAM research questions, partner roles and a roadmap linking AM security requirements, regulatory alignment and technical development. It contributes a research programme that blockchain and MPC protect compromised AM systems.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S3 scope spans design-data sharing and manufacturing workflows.
Threat Model: Prospective project discusses IP theft, manipulation, disruption and sabotage across connected AM supply chains. A complete attacker access/capability model and demonstrated intrusion are not reported.
Purdue Stage: L5 collaboration and authorization, L3 design/build data sharing, L2–L0 manufacturing context
Paper Limitations: Short project roadmap; no completed prototype, attacks or empirical defense evaluation. Proposed blockchain/MPC controls have unestablished practical effectiveness.

Paper Name: Securing Additive Manufacturing with Blockchain-Based Cryptographic Anchoring and Dual-Lock Integrity Auditing
Attacks Mentioned: Models counterfeit products and theft or alteration of outsourced G-code by untrusted storage nodes or coordinators. Keys, management services and the permissioned blockchain trust assumptions bound the adversary; infrastructure compromise is insufficiently evaluated.
Defence Mentioned: SAM-BCADA binds product identifiers and fingerprints to blockchain records using crypto anchors, encryption and signatures. Homomorphic verifiable tags support challenge-based auditing of distributed off-chain G-code; access-controlled retrieval and product verification complete the proposed workflow.
Contribution: Implements a Hyperledger Fabric/IPFS testbed and reports computation, storage and audit-performance measurements. Aerospace deployment is illustrative, with measurements drawn from the controlled virtual environment. The paper explicitly identifies limited adversarial and real-world testing; file integrity and tag authenticity do not independently establish physical part quality.
Lifecycle stage: S1 authorization and provenance, S2 stored G-code integrity, and proposed S5 product-authenticity verification.
Threat Model: Models untrusted storage nodes/coordinators capable of stealing or changing outsourced G-code and counterfeit production. Assumes keys and management services remain trusted and permissioned blockchain assumptions hold; attack robustness against compromised infrastructure is not established.
Purdue Stage: L5 identity/access and shared provenance services; L3 off-chain G-code storage and integrity auditing; L2–L0 product-authentication context.
Paper Limitations: Authors note real-world and adversarial testing limits. VM/container testbed; key secrecy and trusted management assumed, physical-anchor cloning resistance untested; digital file integrity does not prove part quality.

Paper Name: Securing Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing Systems by In-Situ Process Authentication Using Streamline Video Analysis
Attacks Mentioned: Simulates sabotage by rotating infill orientation or introducing an unwanted hollow feature through altered STL/slicing inputs. These changes affect printing paths; the experiment does not demonstrate initial cyber intrusion.
Defence Mentioned: Authenticates layers using a nozzle-mounted microscope video stream. Adaptive texture extraction constructs layer-wise descriptor tensors, multilinear PCA reduces features, and a Hotelling control chart flags departures from nominal builds.
Contribution: Evaluates an optical monitoring method under varying contrast and illumination, comparing detection and computation with a texture-feature benchmark. Four fabricated parts provide nominal and altered layers; processing time supports layer-wise online use under the tested settings.
Lifecycle stage: S2: modeled design/slicing alterations; S3: camera acquisition and online layer authentication.
Threat Model: Sabotage is emulated through altered STL/slicing inputs producing rotated infill or unwanted hollow features. Initial compromise route, attacker identity and access are not demonstrated; nominal reference builds are assumed.
Purdue Stage: L3 design/slicing inputs and baseline; L2 video acquisition/statistical anomaly analysis; L0 nozzle-mounted microscope and physical print.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify parameter variation, wider geometries, sensitivity and other AM processes as future work.

Paper Name: Security Analysis of Networked 3D Printers
Attacks Mentioned: Tests a network-only adversary against 13 printers, demonstrating availability failures, spoofing opportunities, unauthenticated commands, malformed-input crashes, and exposed vulnerable services. It also models multistage paths through surrounding networks; these paths depend on assumed device compromises.
Defence Mentioned: C3PO assesses transfer security, application behavior, availability, exposed services, and deployment attack paths. Findings motivate authentication, encryption, reduced service exposure, and network isolation; it is an assessment tool rather than a runtime prevention system.
Contribution: Introduces a protocol-agnostic network security analysis approach spanning desktop and industrial printers, plus five real deployments. Empirical printer tests and scenario-based network analyses show that deployment weaknesses compound insecure device controls.
Lifecycle stage: S1/S2: unauthorized job access and design/command transfer; S3: printer control, availability, and network exposure during operation.
Threat Model: Network-only adversary sends unauthenticated commands or malformed input, targets exposed services and availability, and may spoof devices. Wider multi-stage paths assume additional network/device compromises; stealth/evasion is outside study.
Purdue Stage: L5/L4 surrounding enterprise/site deployments where analyzed; L3 job/command transfer; L2 network-accessible printer services; L1 printer controller.
Paper Limitations: Authors exclude stealth/evasion and analyze selected tested printers and networks.

Paper Name: Security Analysis of the 3MF Data Format
Attacks Mentioned: An attacker distributes a malicious 3MF file that a victim application opens. XML/OPC parsing and inconsistent interpretation enable data exfiltration, denial of service, or different displayed models across applications, without preinstalled malware or network compromise.
Defence Mentioned: Recommends strict parsing, disabling unsafe XML features, correct OPC relationship processing, external-resource restrictions, and resource limits. Responsible disclosure resulted in some vendor fixes; these outcomes are version- and reporting-date-specific.
Contribution: Systematizes 3MF attack surfaces and implements 3MF Analyzer to generate and evaluate 352 test cases across 20 applications. The study demonstrates application-level format risks; it explicitly excludes discrepancies between one application’s displayed internal model and its printed output.
Lifecycle stage: S1: intake/opening of untrusted model files; S2: model parsing and slicer preparation.
Threat Model: Attacker supplies a malicious 3MF file that a victim opens, exploiting parsing or interpretation discrepancies for exfiltration, denial of service or cross-application model spoofing; no preinstalled malware or network compromise assumed.
Purdue Stage: L5 enterprise model-file intake and application access; L3 model parsing and slicer preparation.
Paper Limitations: Authors restrict study to Windows applications and selected versions and exclude within-application view-versus-print inconsistencies.

Paper Name: Security Challenges of Additive Manufacturing with Metals and Alloys
Attacks Mentioned: Analyzes potential attacks through supply chains, firmware updates, malicious input files, model modification, and process specifications. Manipulating orientation, layer properties, heat delivery, timing, atmosphere, or postprocessing could degrade metal parts or damage equipment.
Defence Mentioned: No implemented or evaluated defense is presented. The chapter motivates security measures informed by materials science and proposes future quantification of effort, consequences, and attack-propagation descriptions.
Contribution: Connects cyber entry points with manufacturing parameters and physical consequences using engineering literature. It extends AM security reasoning beyond visible geometry to microstructure, reliability, machine damage, and manufacturing-environment hazards.
Lifecycle stage: S1: model intake/supply-chain trust; S2: orientation and process preparation; S3: machine parameters and atmosphere; S4: explicit postprocessing and cooling manipulation.
Threat Model: Qualitative analysis considers malicious supply-chain actors, file/firmware manipulation and changed metal process or postprocessing settings to damage equipment or weaken parts; access and capability vary by scenario, with no single tested adversary.
Purdue Stage: L5 file/supply-chain handling; L3 process/orientation preparation; L1–L0 machine, atmosphere and postprocessing equipment.
Paper Limitations: Authors propose quantifying attack effort and consequences as future work.

Paper Name: Security features embedded in computer aided design (CAD) solid models for additive manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Addresses unauthorized printing from stolen CAD designs, assuming the adversary lacks the legitimate processing recipe. It does not prevent file theft or demonstrate an intrusion.
Defence Mentioned: Embeds curved split surfaces and internal geometric features so that STL resolution, slicing and build orientation determine whether they disappear or become defects. Correct processing conditions are retained separately as an additional anti-counterfeiting barrier.
Contribution: CAD-to-print experiments show parameter-dependent discontinuities and support-material inclusions in simple specimens. The work demonstrates fabrication effects, rather than quantified resistance to an informed counterfeiter; knowledgeable users may identify features and industrial validation remains future work. Security depends on software, printer and recipe behaviour.
Lifecycle stage: S1 design embeds protection; S2 conversion and slicing select the recipe; S3 fabrication realizes the conditional features.
Threat Model: Unauthorized manufacturer obtains protected CAD but lacks legitimate conversion, slicing and build parameters and seeks to print a sound counterfeit; no intrusion or prevention of file theft is demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L5 CAD design and access; L3 STL conversion, slicing and recipe; L1–L0 printing realizes embedded physical defects.
Paper Limitations: Authors note knowledgeable users may identify features and further industrial validation is needed. Simple geometries and specific software/printer

Paper Name: Security Implications of Malicious G-Codes in 3D Printing
Attacks Mentioned: Systematizes information disclosure, denial of service, and model manipulation through G-code, including limited access before a victim’s job, malicious slicer configuration, and runtime injection. Persistent settings can affect later jobs without modifying their complete toolpaths.
Defence Mentioned: Implements a G-code scanner for files and supported printer commands. Proposes restricting dangerous commands, resetting configurations between jobs, separating control privileges, and standardizing security practices
Contribution: Combines documented-command analysis and real-world command usage with proof-of-concept tests on four printers and four control boards. It demonstrates that shared printing/configuration privileges enable attacks under weaker adversary capabilities than full firmware compromise.
Lifecycle stage: S1/S2: untrusted job/configuration intake and preprint scanning; S3: printer configuration, command execution, and effects on subsequent prints.
Threat Model: An attacker with limited ability to submit G-code or change slicer settings injects malicious persistent commands before or during victim jobs, seeking data disclosure, denial of service or physical manipulation. Full firmware compromise is not required.
Purdue Stage: L3 untrusted slicer/configuration and build files; L2 printer job/control interfaces and proposed scanning; L1 firmware/command execution; L0 physical printer effects where tested.
Paper Limitations: Authors bound hazardous testing and note firmware/configuration dependence.Some findings rely on command behavior rather than completed attack prints; control-board tests omit mechanical components.

Paper Name: Security of Additive Manufacturing: Attack Taxonomy and Survey
University: University of South Alabama, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Livermore, CA
Attacks Mentioned: Surveys technical-data theft and sabotage through compromised actors, files, software, firmware, networks and physical supplies. Its causal taxonomy connects access vectors, compromised elements, feasible manipulations, resulting effects and adversarial goals; it introduces no new attack experiment.
Defence Mentioned: Reviews protected data streaming, embedded design features, physical fingerprints, in-situ monitoring and post-build inspection. Discussed limitations include local recovery of streamed data, sensor dependence, inspection cost and incomplete defect detectability; these are heterogeneous published approaches rather than a jointly evaluated defence.
Contribution: Organizes AM-specific threats and countermeasures in a common semantic framework. It identifies limited industrial-metal evidence, concentration on desktop polymer printing, and insufficiently comparable detection thresholds and metrics. Reported experimental findings belong to the surveyed studies.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S5 review coverage spans design access, build preparation, fabrication, actual heat treatment/finish machining, and quality inspection. Coverage is analytical and bibliographic, not an experimentally secured end-to-end workflow.
Threat Model: Survey organizes adversary goals, access vectors, compromised components and manipulations across IP theft and sabotage; attacker capabilities vary by cited study. No single operational threat model or new attack experiment is claimed.
Purdue Stage: Literature scope includes L5 enterprise design/supply chain, L3 preparation, L2–L0 execution, finishing and inspection. These are reviewed conceptual locations, not a demonstrated end-to-end secure architecture.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify limited industrial-metal evidence and non-comparable metrics.

Paper Name: Security of Cyber-Physical Additive Manufacturing Supply Chain: Survey, Attack Taxonomy and Solutions
Attacks Mentioned: Surveys IP theft, unauthorized production, sabotage, data breaches and disruption across AM supply-chain activities. Examples include design/toolpath changes, material substitution and equipment manipulation. The aerospace company scenario is an illustrative attack narrative, not a verified incident or measured experiment.
Defence Mentioned: Discusses access control, encryption, intrusion/anomaly detection, threat intelligence and blockchain traceability, with recommended combinations for supply-chain resilience. The paper does not implement or quantitatively validate a new defensive system; suggested benefits remain proposals or findings attributed to reviewed literature.
Contribution: Presents a PRISMA-guided literature review and an expanded taxonomy relating adversary goals, targets and methods to supply-chain stages. The narrative case illustrates applying the taxonomy but supplies no experimental dataset or comparative effectiveness results.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S5 review scope includes design and procurement, preparation, manufacturing, actual surface/thermal postprocessing and quality checks. Distribution and returns extend beyond these AM production stages.
Threat Model: Survey considers insider/outsider IP theft, unauthorized production, sabotage, data breaches and disruption across AM supply chains. Access and capabilities vary across examples; aerospace scenario is illustrative, not an independently verified incident.
Purdue Stage: Literature spans L5–L4 design/procurement and authorization, L3 preparation, L2–L0 build, postprocessing and inspection.
Paper Limitations: PRISMA-guided review and simulated scenario; no new attack experiment, implemented defense or measured comparative effectiveness.

Paper Name: See No Evil, Hear No Evil, Feel No Evil, Print No Evil? Malicious Fill Patterns Detection in Additive Manufacturing
University: Georgia Institute of Technology, Rutgers University
Attacks Mentioned: * Acoustic and spatial verification attack
Contribution: * verification of de_x0002_sign specifications, manufacturing parameters, and materials used in an AM.
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Adversary can manipulate printer firmware or controller PC to change object specifications, manufacturing parameters or source materials; independent sensing is designed not to trust the printer's control stack.
Purdue Stage: L1 firmware/controller and L0 physical printing/materials; L2 independent acoustic/spatial monitoring; L0/2 postproduction material inspection.
Paper Limitations: Authors state the three methods are complementary, not universal verification. Sselected three printers, one CNC machine and tested error patterns do not establish detection of all attacks.

Paper Name: Side Channels of Cyber-Physical Systems: Case Study in Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Side-channel attacks
Contribution:
* analog emissions such as vibration, acoustic, magnetic, and power are analyzed
* proof of concept for the necessity of exploring different analog emissions of CPS that are capable of leaking information
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: Attacker learns side-channel mappings using known G/M-code and a similar printer, then observes target printer emissions to infer geometry. The source discusses acoustic, power, magnetic and vibration signals; the training and target access are attack assumptions.
Purdue Stage: L3 targeted G/M-code/geometry; L1 motor control and L0 process emissions measured during printing. This is a confidentiality case study, not a network compromise.
Paper Limitations: Studied FDM setup, side-channel and estimation conditions constrain generalization; accessing a similar model and target emissions is required. The article does not establish recovery of arbitrary designs under all environmental conditions.

Paper Name: Simulating cyber-physical systems: Identifying vulnerabilities for design and manufacturing through simulated additive manufacturing environments
Attacks Mentioned: Simulates a CAD-level internal pyramidal void that leaves external faces unchanged, then carries the altered design through slicing into a digital FFF build. This is an attack-effect simulation, not a machine-compromise demonstration.
Defence Mentioned: Provides a G-code-driven MATLAB testbed with sampled printer tolerances for evaluating inspection methods. Simulated mass and micrometer inspections fail to distinguish the selected void attack
Contribution: Compares thirty physical Prusa i3 MK3 PLA tensile bars with thirty simulated counterparts using mass, dimensions and scanned geometry. Reported nonsignificant differences support the tested configuration but do not prove universal equivalence. Other machines and human-training benefits require further validation.
Lifecycle stage: S1 design alteration and S2 slicing/simulation are represented, with S3 fabrication modeled and physically validated. S5 mass and dimensional inspection are explicitly assessed in simulation.
Threat Model: Assumes adversary can alter a CAD model by adding an internal void while keeping exterior unchanged. Attack propagation is simulated through slicing and printing; actual compromise path and attacker access are not demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L5 design modification, L3 slicing and simulated G-code, L1–L0 physical/simulated printing and metrology. Inspection tests target part measurement, not proven network compromise.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify limited testbed and future validation needs. One printer/material/specimen, simulated malicious-case inspection, and validation of geometry/mass rather than comprehensive mechanical-strength prediction.

Paper Name: SL1C3D: Slicer Library Injection for Covert 3D Data
Attacks Mentioned: Demonstrates compromised PrusaSlicer libraries that embed covert character strokes in internal infill while displaying a benign preview. Library compromise is the starting assumption; the attack conceals changed G-code inside an apparently ordinary printed object.
Defence Mentioned: A positioning-mode heuristic and independent trusted G-code viewers expose the proof of concept, with acknowledged evasion limits. Bound provenance, reproducible slicing, and independent physical monitoring are proposed broader mitigations.
Contribution: Implements G-code embedding and preview substitution on Windows/PrusaSlicer, then prints PLA objects on a Prusa MK4S. Evaluation reports visual stealth and small resource overhead; mechanical equivalence and robust resistance to specialized inspection are not established by those observations.
Lifecycle stage: S2: slicer compromise, toolpath generation, and deceptive preview; S3: embedded infill execution.
Threat Model: Attacker is assumed able to replace PrusaSlicer libraries; altered slicer embeds covert characters in infill/toolpath and shows benign preview. Aim is covert data embedding; initial library compromise is not demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L3 slicer library, toolpath and preview manipulation; L1–L0 printer execution and embedded infill.
Paper Limitations: Authors discuss bypass limits of preview checks and future broader encodings. Single software/printer configuration, proof-of-concept character strokes detectable in independent preview

Paper Name: SOK: 3D Printer Firmware Attacks on Fused Filament Fabrication
University: Virginia State University, Virginia Commonwealth University
Attacks Mentioned:
1. Object Geometry (OG) Stealing
2. Print Your Own Grave (PYOG) Attack
3. Incurable: Printing Faults Impersonation
4. Object Feature (OF) Scaling
5. Axial Misalignment
6. Internal Cavity Attack
7. Object Density Variation Attack
8. Filament Erosion Attack
9. Printing Facility Air-quality
Defence Mentioned:
* encryption and blockchain technology to ensure data integrity
* lightweight cryptographic solutions such as Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) and the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) provide suitable encryption and authentication services
*  secure communication protocols, like TLS, should be implemented to encrypt data exchanges involving the printer, for MITM attack
* cryptographic signing of firmware files, secure boot mechanisms, and the integration of hardware-based security modules like TPM (Trusted Platform Module) or HSM (Hardware Security Mod_x0002_ule) should be implemented.
Contribution:
* Investigated 48 attacks 
* Proposed 9 attacks, 
* Classification tree for the firmware attacks on 3D printers
* Proposed Attack Feasibility Index (AFI)
Lifecycle stage: Design -> Slicing -> Printing
Threat Model: Assumes malicious firmware installed on an FFF printer; demonstrates nine attacks aiming at surveillance, denial of service and integrity harm to parts, printer or surroundings. The analysis compares 48 attacks across design, slicing and firmware placement.
Purdue Stage: L5 CAD design context, L3 slicing/G-code, L1 compromised firmware and L0 printing, equipment and emissions.
Paper Limitations: Experiments on a standard FFF printer and nine attacks; feasibility scoring and 48-attack comparison are analytical and not proof each attack works on every platform.

Paper Name: SoK: Identifying and Unifying Limitations, Security Threats & Vulnerabilities in Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews technical-data theft and sabotage through software/firmware weaknesses, unprotected communications, side-channel leakage, geometry or parameter changes, and manipulated feedback. Targets include manufactured parts, equipment and the surrounding environment. Attacks and reported outcomes are drawn from cited studies, not new experiments.
Defence Mentioned: Surveys provenance and access-control frameworks, watermarking, acoustic and visual monitoring, piezoelectric inspection, and toolpath-based finite-element checking. Recommends stronger authentication and protected network exposure; individual methods have sensor, material and reference-data constraints, with no combined defence evaluated.
Contribution: Systematizes AM production constraints, attack methods, protective mechanisms and industrial security concerns. It connects machine/material and quality-control limitations to security and calls for a general authentication/access-control framework. This v3 preprint is a narrative synthesis, not a new implementation or comparative benchmark.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S5 review scope spans design/data access, slicing and process planning, build execution, actual heat treatment/finishing, and finished-part inspection.
Threat Model: User-approved v3 survey synthesizes data theft and sabotage through access, communications, firmware, sensors and process changes. Attacker type, access and capabilities vary by cited study; it does not specify a single tested adversary.
Purdue Stage: Literature spans L5 design and access, L3 slicing/preparation, and L2–L0 build, finishing and inspection.

Paper Name: SoK: Side Channel Monitoring for Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Reviews malicious FFF-process deviations alongside ordinary quality defects, including geometry, extrusion, temperature, timing, and layer changes. Side-channel IP theft is contextual; the paper’s main focus is monitoring sabotage and process quality, not a new attack.
Defence Mentioned: Systematizes acoustic, current, thermal, optical, laser, pressure, vibration, and heterogeneous sensing methods, distinguishing per-object profiling from setup-level or profile-free approaches. Discusses noise, calibration, sensor intrusion, precision, and sensor-fusion tradeoffs.
Contribution: Bridges cybersecurity and quality-assurance literature through mappings among process parameters, anomalies, sensing, analysis methods, and reported performance. Recommends shared benchmarks, lower profiling burden, protected monitoring systems, and study of subtle deviations; no new detector is experimentally validated.
Lifecycle stage: Primarily S3: in-process sensing and anomaly detection. S2 reference models support reviewed methods;
Threat Model: Survey covers malicious FFF process changes and benign defects, plus contextual IP side channels. Attacker access and capabilities vary across referenced studies; no single new threat model or attack is executed.
Purdue Stage: Primarily L0 sensors/physical emissions and L2 monitoring/analysis; L1 process actuation and L3 trusted reference preparation where covered by surveyed methods.
Paper Limitations: Authors highlight calibration/noise, profiling burden, benchmarking and sensing tradeoffs.

Paper Name: Spatiotemporal G-code Modeling for Secure FDM-Based 3D Printing
Attacks Mentioned: Evaluates sixteen classes of manipulated G-code affecting nozzle motion, filament kinetics, layer changes, timing, infill, and nozzle/bed temperature. Cyber access is assumed; attacks are enacted by changing instructions supplied to the printer.
Defence Mentioned: Sophos compares trusted G-code-derived spatial and temporal profiles with independent optical-encoder and temperature measurements. Layer-wise checks examine geometry, extrusion, motion, timing, and temperature, identifying deviations beyond calibrated tolerances.
Contribution: Provides multiattribute G-code modeling and heterogeneous sensing that expose attacks invisible to geometry-only monitoring. The selected attack and benign cases were separated successfully at chosen thresholds; the paper explicitly shows that changes below those thresholds can be missed.
Lifecycle stage: S2: trusted instruction transformation and parameter modeling; S3: independent sensing and layer-by-layer authentication during printing.
Threat Model: Attacker can change G-code before or during delivery to the printer and aims to perturb motion, filament, timing, infill or temperature. Detector assumes trusted G-code and independent calibrated sensing; initial cyber access is assumed.
Purdue Stage: L3 trusted G-code and profile generation; L2 independent sensor acquisition/comparison; L1–L0 motor/temperature control and physical process.
Paper Limitations: Authors note attacks below selected tolerance thresholds can be missed. Requires trusted reference, sensors, calibration and model accuracy; perfect results are limited to selected tests and thresholds.

Paper Name: Spooky Manufacturing: Probabilistic Sabotage Attack in Metal Additive Manufacturing Using Shielding Gas Flow Control
Where When Published: ACM CCS Workshop on Additive Manufacturing Security (AMSec@CCS); 2022
Attacks Mentioned: Analyzes shielding-gas-flow sabotage in laser powder-bed fusion. Insufficient or excessive flow can affect laser attenuation, spatter deposition and powder uniformity, producing probabilistic defects in one or multiple parts. Candidate compromised controllers, sensors and supply-chain entry paths are reasoned, not exploited.
Defence Mentioned: Discusses detectability using inspection and the difficulty of distinguishing sabotage from naturally occurring process defects. No new detector or countermeasure is implemented; experimental attack and NDT validation are future work.
Contribution: Uses manufacturing physics literature and an Open Additive PANDA subsystem analysis to connect controllable gas-flow elements with possible damage. The contribution is a causal attack analysis emphasizing stochastic targeting and attribution limits, without measured attack success probabilities or demonstrated strength loss.
Lifecycle stage: S3: gas-flow control and associated build defects. S5 inspection and witness-coupon implications are discussed analytically
Threat Model: Conceptual adversary manipulates shielding-gas-flow controls, sensors or supply path to cause probabilistic LPBF defects. Initial compromise and exact access are hypothesized, not exploited; no measured success probability.
Purdue Stage: L1 gas-flow control and sensors; L0 gas, powder and physical build; L2–L0 inspection/witness-coupon implications are analytical.
Paper Limitations: Authors defer experimental sabotage and NDT validation. No intrusion, attack-success probability or measured strength loss demonstrated.

Paper Name: State of Security Awareness in the Additive Manufacturing Industry: 2020 Survey
Where When Published: ASTM STP 1644: Progress in Additive Manufacturing 2021; 2022
Attacks Mentioned: Surveys perceived AM threats, adversaries, attacker objectives, outsourcing risks, and reported incidents. IP theft and sabotage are respondent/research concerns; the study neither executes attacks nor establishes their prevalence through independently verified incident data.
Defence Mentioned: Examines reported risk assessments, security programs, external providers, and reliance on general cybersecurity. Recommends AM-specific guidance, better awareness, and information sharing rather than evaluating a technical countermeasure.
Contribution: Reports a 2020 questionnaire with 69 respondents from 64 organizations and 53 complete responses. The analysis finds preparedness and conceptual-understanding gaps among participants, while explicitly cautioning against extrapolating to the whole industry or equating individual answers with organizational knowledge.
Lifecycle stage: S1: organizational risk planning, supplier/outsourcing trust, and security governance.
Threat Model: Questionnaire asks participants about perceived adversaries, IP theft, sabotage, outsourcing and incidents. It does not define or demonstrate a single attacker capability/access model or independently confirm incident reports.
Purdue Stage: L5–L4 enterprise awareness, organizational risk and supplier governance.
Paper Limitations: Authors warn against industry-wide extrapolation and equating answers with organizational knowledge.

Paper Name: Stealthy Cyber Anomaly Detection On Large Noisy Multi-material 3D Printer Datasets Using Probabilistic Models
Where When Published: ACM CCS Workshop on Additive Manufacturing Security (AMSec@CCS); 2022
Attacks Mentioned: Emulates gradual temperature-setpoint changes and small single-command Z-axis changes in a fiber-reinforced polymer printer. Toolpath access is assumed; attack classes target subtle process deviations, and mechanical effects are not uniformly damaging.
Defence Mentioned: Uses filtered, synchronized side-channel current/PWM measurements, phase-synchrony features, and Bayesian logistic classification trained on known-good and attacked runs. Detection varies by sensor and training attack; early real-time deployment remains future work.
Contribution: Demonstrates probabilistic classification on noisy, large multi-material printing datasets and studies transfer across attack classes. It identifies useful cross-actuator signals but acknowledges unexplained causal links, labeled-training requirements, and computational costs. Appendix tests show that some changes have modest or no adverse strength effects.
Lifecycle stage: S2/S3: altered G-code and execution-side monitoring. Mechanical flex tests validate consequences rather than constituting an S5 security workflow;
Threat Model: Attack emulation changes temperature setpoints or a single Z-axis instruction, assuming access to build commands, to produce subtle process deviations. Detector assumes known-good baseline and labeled attacked runs; no initial intrusion demonstrated.
Purdue Stage: L3 toolpath/parameter changes; L1–L0 temperature/Z control and process signals; L2 signal collection and probabilistic monitoring. Mechanical tests evaluate effects, not a deployed certification workflow.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify unexplained cross-actuator signal links, labeled-training requirements and real-time computation as open issues. Offline feasibility on a limited noisy multi-material dataset; effects vary and are not uniformly damaging.

Paper Name: Streaming in Metal Additive Manufacturing: A Catalyst for Secure Distributed Manufacturing
Where When Published: International Journal of Production Research (online 2025; vol. 64 issue 10 in 2026); 2025
Attacks Mentioned: Considers theft and unauthorized reuse of metal-AM production data through interception, redirection, memory extraction and compromised machine software. These are analysed threat scenarios, not demonstrated penetration tests; software that copies decrypted layers can undermine the protection.
Defence Mentioned: Streams parameterized 2.5D vector workplanes instead of transferring the complete job. The implementation combines certificate-authenticated TLS, encrypted payloads, licence-based keys/production counters and restricted layer delivery/buffering to reduce accessible data and control authorized production.
Contribution: Implements a server/client protocol and demonstrates physical streaming manufacture on an Alpha 140 metal powder-bed-fusion machine. Timing measurements show layer delivery fits the tested recoating interval; additional streaming trials examine distributed operation. This establishes feasibility, while security arguments depend on trusted machine-side execution and licensing.
Lifecycle stage: S1 production authorization, S2 preparation of streamable build data and S3 layer delivery/execution.
Threat Model: Threat analysis considers theft, interception, redirection or memory extraction of production data during outsourced metal-AM manufacturing. Authenticated stream assumes trusted machine-side software and license management; a compromised client can copy decrypted workplanes.
Purdue Stage: L5 licensing/authorization and server/client collaboration; L3 prepared layer data and stream generation; L2–L1 client/controller layer delivery; L0 metal printer execution.
Paper Limitations: Authors explicitly note compromised client can copy decrypted workplanes and interruption recovery needs work.

Paper Name: Survey of 3D Printer Security Offensive and Defensive
University: Lanzhou University of Technology, National Computer Network Intrusion Protection Center, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, China
Attacks Mentioned: Surveys attacks by intent: technical-data theft, AM sabotage and illegal-part manufacturing. Reviewed mechanisms include side-channel leakage, geometry/parameter tampering, firmware modification and material manipulation. Illegal manufacturing is explicitly distinguished from an external intrusion against a printer owner.
Defence Mentioned: Groups prior defences into security architectures and attack detection, covering authentication, encryption, access permissions, provenance, acoustic/multimodal monitoring and physical hashing. Published accuracy values describe different underlying studies and are not results of a new common evaluation.
Contribution: Synthesizes offensive and defensive literature and proposes research questions concerning leakage fidelity, realistic sabotage validation, traceability, firmware security and robust sensing. It conducts no original attack or detector experiment; some cited network-printing work is broader than AM.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S3 scope includes data access, model/toolpath preparation and machine execution. S4 finishing appears in a cited workflow;
Threat Model: Survey classifies IP theft, sabotage and illegal manufacture; attacker access and capabilities differ across cited studies. Illegal printing is treated separately from outside compromise of the printer owner.
Purdue Stage: L5 design access, L3 preparation, L2–L0 execution and inspection as reviewed conceptual scope
Paper Limitations: Authors identify realistic sabotage validation, traceability, firmware security and sensing as research questions.

Paper Name: Taxonomies for Reasoning About Cyber-physical Attacks in IoT-based Manufacturing Systems
Where When Published: Int. J. Interact. Multim. Artif. Intell.; 2017
Attacks Mentioned: Classifies manufacturing attacks by vectors, vulnerabilities, targets, and confidentiality/integrity/availability impacts, including material and geometric manipulation. Connects software vulnerabilities to possible manufacturing consequences; case-study paths are reasoned possibilities rather than demonstrated exploit chains.
Defence Mentioned: Pairs attack classes with quality-control checks such as dimensions, CT, strength testing, and side-channel monitoring. Proposed reasoning links plant configuration and vulnerability data to appropriate checks; automated recommendation software remains future work.
Contribution: Offers coordinated attack and quality-control taxonomies, illustrated using an AM service provider’s process and IT infrastructure. It exposes how compromised design, production, or inspection computers can undermine assurance and discusses coverage/cost tradeoffs.
Lifecycle stage: S1: customer design intake; S2: file preparation; S3: machine/process checks; S5: part inspection and vulnerable inspection systems.
Threat Model: Models possible attacks by vector, vulnerability, targets and impacts in an AM service-provider infrastructure, including compromised design, production and inspection computers. Access varies by scenario; paths are reasoned, not demonstrated exploit chains.
Purdue Stage: L5 customer design intake; L3 build preparation; L2–L0 process control and quality inspection.
Paper Limitations: Authors propose automated recommendation as future work. Conceptual attack-to-QC mappings with no quantified detection effectiveness or deployed recommendation engine.

Paper Name: Taxonomy-Driven Graph-Theoretic Framework for Manufacturing Cybersecurity Risk Modeling and Assessment
University: The University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ
Attacks Mentioned: Models possible manufacturing attacks as paths from entry vectors through affected locations to consequences. The illustrative manufacturing-as-a-service case considers hardware tampering and man-in-the-middle access affecting part quality; it does not execute these attacks.
Defence Mentioned: Uses taxonomy-derived directed graphs, exploit/propagation probabilities and consequence costs to estimate risk and prioritize intervention. Authentication, access control and intrusion prevention are represented by revised hypothetical probabilities; resulting risk reductions are model outputs, not measured defensive effectiveness.
Contribution: Connects a six-component risk taxonomy to attack-path enumeration and weighted-graph analysis. A hybrid additive/subtractive manufacturing scenario demonstrates calculations and how controls change prioritized paths. Probability estimation is outside scope, so conclusions depend strongly on assumed inputs and graph structure.
Lifecycle stage: Conceptual S1 design intake, S2 production instructions, S3 machine operation and S5 dimensional inspection occur in the illustrative workflow.
Threat Model: Illustrative manufacturing-as-a-service scenario models hardware tampering and man-in-the-middle attacks, assuming graph paths and numerical exploit/propagation probabilities; attackers seek part-quality impact. No intrusion is executed.
Purdue Stage: L5 design/customer access, L3 manufacturing instruction preparation, L1–L0 machine hardware and part production,
Paper Limitations: Authors leave probability estimation and dynamic graph updates to future work.

Paper Name: Thermal Side-Channel Forensics in Additive Manufacturing Systems
Attacks Mentioned: Side-channel attack -> THERMAL FORENSICS
Lifecycle stage: Printing
Threat Model: An observer uses thermal images of additive manufacturing to infer printing parameters and potentially geometry; exact placement, access and reconstruction capabilities require the poster text.
Purdue Stage: L0 thermal emissions during printing and L3 exposed digital instructions;

Paper Name: Threat modelling for industrial cyber physical systems in the era of smart manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Models industrial-control threats by linking actors, assets, vulnerabilities, attack techniques, and consequences. Attack trees and risk rankings are developed for a Festo automotive-production test rig, rather than demonstrated AM sabotage.
Defence Mentioned: Integrates threat modeling with VueOne digital-twin metadata and Siemens engineering tools. A prototype generates selected mitigation policies, configuration, and control code; risk prioritization supports choosing defenses but is not evidence of measured resistance to attacks.
Contribution: Presents a structured methodology and tool for asset criticality, threat analysis, qualitative/quantitative risk assessment, and mitigation generation during industrial-system engineering. The case study demonstrates tool integration and workflow feasibility; broader attack simulation and human-factor analysis remain future work.
Lifecycle stage: General ICPS design and operation are covered. An AM-specific S1–S5 mapping is not established because the validation concerns an automotive test rig rather than an additive-manufacturing workflow.
Threat Model: Threat modeling considers actors, vulnerabilities and industrial control-system consequences in an automotive production test rig; access varies by modeled attack tree. No AM-specific attack or attacker capabilities established.
Purdue Stage: General ICPS case concerns Festo automotive rig and associated engineering/control systems

Paper Name: TMAP: A Threat Modeling and Attack Path Analysis Framework for Industrial IoT Systems (A Case Study of IoM and IoP)
Where When Published: Arabian Journal for Science and Engineering; 2023
University: Indian Institute of Information Technology, Allahabad
Attacks Mentioned: Models spoofing, tampering, disclosure, denial of service and privilege escalation across IIoT assets and communications. Manufacturing HMI and electric-power SCADA cases illustrate attack paths; these are modeled possibilities, not executed intrusions.
Defence Mentioned: Combines Purdue architecture, data-flow diagrams, asset identification, STRIDE, MITRE ATT&CK-informed paths and CVSS prioritization. The output supports security planning; no deployed detector or measured mitigation effectiveness is established.
Contribution: Provides a six-step workflow and two worked industrial cases with threat counts and vulnerability rankings. Counts describe modeling outputs, while CVSS scores express vulnerability severity rather than observed attack likelihood. Financial-loss prediction and broader risk assessment remain future work.
Lifecycle stage: No AM lifecycle stage is established. The cases address general manufacturing and electric-power control systems, without an additive-manufacturing process demonstration.
Threat Model: STRIDE-based IIoT modeling considers spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, denial of service and privilege escalation; manufacturing HMI and power SCADA attack paths are hypothetical, not executed. No AM-specific adversary established.
Purdue Stage: not an AM demonstration.

Paper Name: Tool of Spies: Leaking Your Intellectual Property by Altering the Compiler
Where When Published: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing; 2019
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes one-time access to alter the CAM compiler plus nearby sensing and profiling on the target or a similar printer. Compiler-inserted parameter changes amplify acoustic, vibration, electromagnetic or power leakage so an attacker can infer geometric instructions more easily.
Defence Mentioned: Proposes leakage reduction, G/M-code verification, trusted toolchain references and shielding. These are countermeasure directions, not evaluated defensive implementations.
Contribution: Implements compiler alterations and measures improved inference of line angles, layer changes and segment boundaries using learned models. Tests focus on desktop FDM and polygonal shapes, analyzing channels individually. Reported relative improvement should not be confused with complete design recovery; curved geometry, combined channels and industrial printers require further study.
Lifecycle stage: S2: compiler/toolpath preparation introduces leakage-enhancing instructions. S3: physical emissions are captured during fabrication to infer design information.
Threat Model: Attacker obtains one-time access to the CAM compiler and nearby sensing/profiling on the target or similar printer. Compiler-inserted parameter changes enhance acoustic, vibration, electromagnetic or power leakage to infer geometry.
Purdue Stage: L3 compiler/toolpath preparation; L1 motor/firmware actuation; L0 physical emissions and nearby sensors.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify curved geometry, combined channels and industrial printers as future work. Desktop FDM and polygon shapes, strong compiler/sensor access, no demonstrated arbitrary-object full reconstruction;

Paper Name: Turning Hearsay into Discovery: Industrial 3D Printer Side Channel Information Translated to Stealing the Object Design
Attacks Mentioned: A malicious manufacturer or insider with physical access instruments laser current and galvanometer position-output voltages to reconstruct printed designs. Demonstrated on a Sintratec S2 polymer powder-bed-fusion machine; this is privileged internal measurement, not remote eavesdropping.
Defence Mentioned: Discusses side-channel risk mitigation and proposes using the same measurements for future sabotage detection and localization. No confidentiality countermeasure or sabotage detector is evaluated.
Contribution: Builds voxel models from layer-separated actuator traces, then prunes, fills and corrects distortion. Two geometries demonstrate design recovery; combining three specimen traces improves reconstruction. Results depend on geometry-specific filling and calibration, and experimental proportion correction uses original STL dimensions, limiting claims of fully blind recovery. Metal PBF applicability is inferred from shared mechanisms, not experimentally tested.
Lifecycle stage: S3: information leakage is captured during build execution. Design confidentiality is the protected asset;
Threat Model: Malicious manufacturer/insider with privileged physical access instruments laser current and galvanometer position test points to reconstruct printed geometry. No remote eavesdropping is demonstrated; calibration and original STL dimensions are used in experimental correction.
Purdue Stage: L1 galvanometer/laser control outputs and L0 actuator signals/material process; recovered design is an L3 information asset.
Paper Limitations: Authors acknowledge geometry-dependent processing and limited industrial generalization.Two full-infill geometries on one polymer PBF platform; original STL dimensions aid proportion correction, so fully blind recovery not established.

Paper Name: Using 3D printers as weapons
University: University of South Alabama, Auburn University
Attacks Mentioned: Conceptually examines compromised AM workflows causing harmful physical effects through altered materials, object specifications, manufacturing parameters or postprocessing. Targets include parts, equipment and their environment. The authors explicitly characterize the attack examples as primarily hypothetical and requiring experimental or real-world confirmation.
Defence Mentioned: Discusses integrity protection, physical/cyber access restrictions and firmware/hardware safety checks as constraints on feasible manipulation. These are general protective considerations, not a newly implemented or evaluated defence; compromised low-level components can bypass assumed safeguards.
Contribution: Provides linked taxonomies of compromised elements, manipulations and harmful outcomes, plus qualitative characteristics including targeting precision, impact area, collateral damage, stealth and repeatability. It concerns misuse of manufacturing systems to cause harm, rather than a study of manufacturing conventional weapons.
Lifecycle stage: S1–S4 coverage includes supply/design access, object and process specifications, fabrication, and actual hot-isostatic-pressing/postprocessing parameters.
Threat Model: Hypothetical attacker controls selected compromised workflow elements and manipulates materials, object specifications, processes or postprocessing to produce harmful parts, equipment or environmental outcomes. Coordinated attacks are outside the developed taxonomy.
Purdue Stage: L5 supply/design; L3 object and process specifications; L1–L0 fabrication and postprocessing controls/physical process.
Paper Limitations: Authors characterize attacks primarily as hypothetical, assume full control of a compromised element and exclude coordinated attacks.

Paper Name: Vulnerabilities and Attacks on CAN-Based 3D Printing/Additive Manufacturing
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes one compromised CAN node or a malicious replacement module. Unauthenticated shared traffic enables sniffing, spoofed commands and sensor feedback, and denial of service. A microcontroller on a commercial printer’s CAN hub injects false temperature reports, causing shutdown; additional control and safety manipulations are reported.
Defence Mentioned: Calls for CAN security adapted to frequently exchanged, plug-and-play AM modules and discusses existing automotive approaches. No implemented or experimentally evaluated defensive protocol is supplied.
Contribution: Translates CAN weaknesses into private, safety-critical and security-data risks for modular printers, and presents a practical bus-access attack demonstration. The illustrated temperature-spoofing experiment is stronger evidence than generalized claims about all printers or entire farms.
Lifecycle stage: S3: module initialization, machine calibration, sensor feedback and build-time actuation.
Threat Model: Attacker compromises or replaces a CAN node, or attaches a malicious device to a shared bus; unauthenticated traffic permits sniffing, spoofed commands/sensor feedback and denial of service. Temperature spoofing is demonstrated with physical bus access.
Purdue Stage: L1 CAN-connected controller/modules and shared control communications; L0 temperature sensor and physical printer; L2 operator-visible machine status where applicable.
Paper Limitations: One commercial printer and physically attached node; other discussed attacks have less experimental detail than temperature spoofing.

Paper Name: Watching and Safeguarding Your 3D Printer: Online Process Monitoring Against Cyber-Physical Attacks
Where When Published: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies; 2018
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes malicious printer firmware that alters infill paths, printing speed, layer thickness or cooling-fan operation while retaining apparently normal exterior features. Experiments introduce these changes directly; an initial firmware-compromise exploit is not demonstrated.
Defence Mentioned: Reconstructs physical printing attributes using accelerometers, a magnetometer, camera images and audio, then compares them with G-code expectations. Kalman filtering, image-edge analysis and acoustic classification support online deviation detection.
Contribution: Evaluates four attack classes on an Ultimaker, with additional path and fan-speed evaluation on a Lulzbot. Demonstrates independent physical monitoring, but reported perfect attack identification concerns selected significant distortions. Small changes near critical structures, nonprinting travel and changing magnetic interference remain limitations; deployment requires calibration.
Lifecycle stage: S3: in-process monitoring of motion, deposition and cooling. S2 G-code supplies the reference;
Threat Model: Assumed malicious firmware changes infill, speed, layer height or fan operation to alter the physical part. Experiments directly introduce deviations; firmware infection is not demonstrated. Detector assumes trusted expected G-code and calibrated sensors.
Purdue Stage: L3 trusted expected G-code; L2 independent camera/audio/signal processing; L1 firmware and controller; L0 motion, deposition and cooling signals.
Paper Limitations: Authors identify magnetic interference, small critical deviations and nonprinting travel as challenges. Limited printer/attack cases, sensor calibration and stable interference conditions required; selected-case performance is not universal.

Paper Name: WattShield: A Power Side-Channel Framework for Detecting Malicious Firmware in Fused Filament Fabrication
Attacks Mentioned: Assumes compromised Marlin firmware and implements nine previously described scenarios targeting design secrecy, printer/facility conditions and printed geometry or temperature. Firmware infiltration is an assumed prerequisite, not an experimentally demonstrated entry exploit.
Defence Mentioned: WattShield measures aggregate supply current with an independent monitor. An activity classifier and thermal estimation compare observations with G-code expectations. Object sabotage triggers alerts; IP theft and environmental sabotage are exposed through activity logs requiring manual interpretation.
Contribution: Evaluates the framework on an Ultimaker2+ without a per-object reference print, while retaining printer-specific training and calibration. It separates thermal and motion evidence, but cannot directly monitor extrusion; sufficiently small changes can evade thresholds. Prediction accuracy is distinct from attack-detection coverage.
Lifecycle stage: S3: printer preparation, build execution and associated activity monitoring. S2 G-code is the trusted comparison input, without a demonstrated slicer-stage defence.
Threat Model: Compromised Marlin firmware is assumed and nine known scenarios are implemented to threaten geometry, temperature, IP or surroundings; initial infection is not demonstrated. Monitor uses trusted G-code and printer-specific calibration/training.
Purdue Stage: L3 trusted G-code reference; L2 independent current monitoring and inference; L1 firmware/controller; L0 measured supply current and printer activity.
Paper Limitations: Authors note pure extrusion and subthreshold changes may evade sensing, and IP/environmental cases require manual log review.
